Techniques To Eliminate Confounders

Method

Description

Matching


 
  • Cases are matched with the control and should be similar to the control in every possible variable that can affect the study's outcome except the disease in question.
  • Done in a case-control study.
  • Eliminates only the known confounders.

Restriction

  • Limits participation in the study to individuals who are similar in terms of confounders.

Randomisation

  • The technique where every participant will get an equal and known chance of being allocated to either the treatment group or the control group.
  • Eliminates both known and unknown confounders.

Stratification (Segregate)

  • Stratify the participants of the study or segregate them.

Standardisation

  • Adjusting the results to a standard population to control for confounding variables often used in rate comparisons
  • Eliminate or control the effect of age and gender.

Multivariate regression models

  • Used when there are multiple confounders.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate high-quality chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute

questions.answerText: Initiate high-quality chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute
questions.solution: Steps Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) is crucial for managing cardiac arrest and cardiovascular emergencies, following the 2016 guidelines. Key Steps in ACLS Step Description 1. Early Recognition and Activation Identify cardiac arrest signs quickly and alert emergency services. 2. High-Quality Chest Compressions (Option C) Initiate compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute, with a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) for adults, allowing full chest recoil. 3. Early Defibrillation (Option D ruled out) Deploy an AED promptly; follow prompts for defibrillation if a shockable rhythm is present. 4. Airway Management (Option B ruled out) Ensure airway patency using techniques like bag-mask ventilation or advanced airway placement; provide oxygen to support ventilation. 5. Drug Administration (Option A ruled out) Administer epinephrine (1 mg every 3-5 minutes); consider antiarrhythmics like amiodarone for shock-resistant VF/pulseless VT. 6. Identify and Treat Reversible Causes Assess for reversible causes ("H's and T's"): Hypoxia Hypovolemia Acidosis (Hydrogen ion) Hyper/hypokalemia Hypothermia Tension pneumothorax Cardiac tamponade Toxins Thrombosis (pulmonary/coronary) 7. Post-Resuscitation Care Provide comprehensive care after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), including monitoring and supportive therapies. 8. Continuous Quality Improvement Assess and enhance resuscitation efforts, focusing on minimizing interruptions in compressions and following protocols. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Steps

Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) is crucial for managing cardiac arrest and cardiovascular emergencies, following the 2016 guidelines.

Key Steps in ACLS

Step

Description

1. Early Recognition and Activation

Identify cardiac arrest signs quickly and alert emergency services.

2. High-Quality Chest Compressions (Option C)

Initiate compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute, with a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) for adults, allowing full chest recoil.

3. Early Defibrillation (Option D ruled out)

Deploy an AED promptly; follow prompts for defibrillation if a shockable rhythm is present.

4. Airway Management (Option B ruled out)

Ensure airway patency using techniques like bag-mask ventilation or advanced airway placement; provide oxygen to support ventilation.

5. Drug Administration (Option A ruled out)

Administer epinephrine (1 mg every 3-5 minutes); consider antiarrhythmics like amiodarone for shock-resistant VF/pulseless VT.

6. Identify and Treat Reversible Causes

Assess for reversible causes ("H's and T's"):

Hypoxia

Hypovolemia

Acidosis (Hydrogen ion)

Hyper/hypokalemia

Hypothermia

Tension pneumothorax

Cardiac tamponade

Toxins

Thrombosis (pulmonary/coronary)

7. Post-Resuscitation Care

Provide comprehensive care after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), including monitoring and supportive therapies.

8. Continuous Quality Improvement

Assess and enhance resuscitation efforts, focusing on minimizing interruptions in compressions and following protocols.

questions.stem: Match the following: 1) Pneumocystis pneumonia a) 2) Blastomycosis b) 3) Aspergillus c) 4) Measles d)
questions.stemHtml: Match the following: 1) Pneumocystis pneumonia a) 2) Blastomycosis b) 3) Aspergillus c) 4) Measles d)
questions.solution: li>Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic fungus that causes Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). PCP primarily affects immunocompromised individuals . Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) staining is the method of choice to demonstrate the cysts of P. jirovecii. The cysts resemble black-coloured crushed ping-pong balls against the green background. Blastomycosis: Blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis found in moist soil. Morphology: In the normal host, the lung lesions of blastomycosis are suppurative granulomas. Macrophages have a limited ability to ingest and kill B. dermatitidis, and the persistence of the yeast cells leads to the recruitment of neutrophils . In tissue, B. dermatitidis is a round, 5- to 15-μm yeast cell divided by broad-based budding. It has a thick, double-contoured cell wall and visible nuclei. Aspergillus: Aspergillosis is an invasive and allergic disease caused by a hyaline mould named Aspergillus. Glucocorticoid use is the most important risk factor for aspergillosis. Pulmonary aspergillosis is the most common form. KOH (10%) mount or histopathological staining of specimens reveals characteristic narrow septate hyaline hyphae with acute angle branching. Measles: The measles virus is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Paramyxoviridae family. It causes measles, an acute, highly contagious childhood disease characterised by fever and respiratory symptoms followed by a typical maculopapular rash. Virus isolation: Cytopathic effect may be observed after 7–10 days of inoculation into cell lines characterised by multinucleated giant cells (Warthin-Finkeldey cells) containing intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. It can cause giant-cell pneumonitis (Hecht’s pneumonia) in immunocompromised children and HIV-infected people. @Neet_pg_bot

le appearance is the characteristic radiological finding of giant cell tumors. It presents as a lytic lesion with multiple internal septations, giving it a soap bubble appearance. It is usually located in the epiphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur.

 

X-ray findings in Giant cell tumors (GCTs):

  • Eccentric location, often subchondral.
  • Expansion of the overlying cortex.
  • The cortex may be thinned out.
  • Lobulated lytic lesions with narrow zones of transition produce a soap bubble appearance. (Option C)

Sun-rays appearance (Option A) seen in osteosarcoma.

Onion peel appearance (Option B)is associated with Ewing's sarcoma

Pepper pot appearance (Option D) is seen in multiple myeloma.

Immunocompromised patients

  • He began a nutritional rehabilitation program to address his malnutrition which led to refeeding syndrome as evidenced by the complication of seizure (involuntary muscle contractions, followed by periods of unresponsiveness and confusion)

    •  

    Refeeding Syndrome

    • Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition that can occur in significantly malnourished patients when they are reintroduced to calories, particularly carbohydrates, after a period of starvation or very low caloric intake.
    • The syndrome is characterized by a series of metabolic and electrolyte disturbances due to the sudden increase in insulin secretion in response to increased calorie intake.

     

    Category

    Details

    Risk Factors
    • Severe malnutrition (e.g., anorexia nervosa, prolonged fasting)
    • Patients who have experienced significant weight loss or are undergoing aggressive refeeding

    Metabolic Changes (Option B, C)

    Increased insulin levels lead to shifts in electrolytes, particularly:

    • Decreased phosphate (PO4³⁻): Essential for energy production and cellular function. Most common electrolyte abnormality seen in this condition; it is accompanied by prolonged QT interval and bradycardia.
    • Decreased potassium (K⁺): Important for cardiac and muscular function.
    • Decreased magnesium (Mg²⁺): Critical for many biochemical reactions and muscle function.

    Clinical Complications
    • Cardiac complications: Arrhythmias due to electrolyte imbalances.
    • Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown caused by electrolyte disturbances and increased workload.
    • Seizures: Can occur due to severe electrolyte imbalances.

    Management

    To prevent refeeding syndrome, it is crucial to:

    • Start feeding at a reduced caloric rate and gradually increase.
    • Monitor electrolytes closely, particularly phosphate, potassium, and magnesium.
    • Provide thiamine supplementation before correcting glucose levels.


     

    Hypernatremia (Option D): This does not align with the rapid weight loss and subsequent neurological disturbances observed in this case.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old female presents for management of her hypertension and heart failure. She has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease (stage 3). The initiation of an ACE inhibitor is considered. Which of the following are the uses of ACE inhibitors in this scenario?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old female presents for management of her hypertension and heart failure. She has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease (stage 3). The initiation of an ACE inhibitor is considered. Which of the following are the uses of ACE inhibitors in this scenario?
questions.solution: The patient has multiple comorbidities that would benefit from the use of ACE inhibitors (ACEIs), including: Reduction of proteinuria: ACEIs help decrease proteinuria, which slows the progression of kidney damage in Chronic Kidney disease (CKD). Reduction of preload and afterload: ACEIs improve symptoms and outcomes in heart failure patients by reducing both preload and afterload on the heart. Prevention of diabetic nephropathy: ACEIs help prevent the progression of diabetic nephropathy by lowering intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration, thereby preventing albuminuria. Uses of ACEI: Hypertension : ACEIs are particularly effective in patients with comorbid conditions such as diabetes, CKD, and scleroderma. Myocardial Infarction (MI) : ACEIs are used both in the acute management of MI and for long-term secondary prophylaxis. Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) : ACEIs improve outcomes by reducing the workload on the heart. Prophylaxis in high cardiovascular-risk individuals : ACEIs protect both the myocardium and vasculature, possibly through improved endothelial function. Scleroderma : ACEIs can prevent the rise in blood pressure and renal function deterioration mediated by angiotensin II in patients with scleroderma. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The patient has multiple comorbidities that would benefit from the use of ACE inhibitors (ACEIs), including:

  • Reduction of proteinuria: ACEIs help decrease proteinuria, which slows the progression of kidney damage in Chronic Kidney disease (CKD).
  • Reduction of preload and afterload: ACEIs improve symptoms and outcomes in heart failure patients by reducing both preload and afterload on the heart.
  • Prevention of diabetic nephropathy: ACEIs help prevent the progression of diabetic nephropathy by lowering intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration, thereby preventing albuminuria.

 

Uses of ACEI:

  • Hypertension: ACEIs are particularly effective in patients with comorbid conditions such as diabetes, CKD, and scleroderma.
  • Myocardial Infarction (MI): ACEIs are used both in the acute management of MI and for long-term secondary prophylaxis.
  • Congestive Heart Failure (CHF): ACEIs improve outcomes by reducing the workload on the heart.
  • Prophylaxis in high cardiovascular-risk individuals: ACEIs protect both the myocardium and vasculature, possibly through improved endothelial function.
  • Scleroderma: ACEIs can prevent the rise in blood pressure and renal function deterioration mediated by angiotensin II in patients with scleroderma.

Cartridge of Rifle

  • Types:
    • Lead bullets: Made entirely of lead, offering expansion upon impact.
    • Metal-Jacketed Bullets: A lead core encased in a metal jacket (usually copper) enhances accuracy and reduces barrel fouling.

questions.solution: ss="customMeta" data-dictid="0338b655da16927771984b872baabb">Spasm (DES) Definition Uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophagus with normal LES function. Clinical Features Dysphagia (solids and liquids) Severe chest pain Less common regurgitation Globus sensation Investigations Esophageal Manometry: Multiple simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions with an amplitude of > 30 mmHg; normal LES pressure and relaxation. Barium Swallow (Esophagram): "Corkscrew" or "Rosary bead" appearance. (Option A) Endoscopy: Generally normal mucosa; rule out structural abnormalities. Management Non-Pharmacological: Dietary Modifications (smaller, frequent meals) Pharmacological: Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., nifedipine) Nitrates (e.g., isosorbide dinitrate) Botulinum Toxin Injection Surgical: Esophageal Myotomy (rare) Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM) Endoscopic: Dilation (less effective) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ss="customMeta" data-dictid="0338b655da16927771984b872baabb">Spasm (DES)

 

Definition

Uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophagus with normal LES function.

Clinical Features
  • Dysphagia (solids and liquids)
  • Severe chest pain
  • Less common regurgitation
  • Globus sensation

Investigations

Esophageal Manometry: Multiple simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions with an amplitude of > 30 mmHg; normal LES pressure and relaxation.
 

Barium Swallow (Esophagram): "Corkscrew" or "Rosary bead" appearance.

(Option A)
 

Endoscopy: Generally normal mucosa; rule out structural abnormalities.

Management

Non-Pharmacological: Dietary Modifications (smaller, frequent meals)
 

Pharmacological:

  • Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., nifedipine)
  • Nitrates (e.g., isosorbide dinitrate)
  • Botulinum Toxin Injection
 

Surgical:

  • Esophageal Myotomy (rare)
  • Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM)
 

Endoscopic: Dilation (less effective)

Management of babies born to HBV-positive mothers:

questions.solution: Correct Option: C) Focal Nodular Hyperplasia FNH is a benign liver lesion commonly found in women and is characterised by a well-defined mass with a central stellate scar, which can sometimes contain calcifications. The presence of these features on imaging is highly suggestive of FNH. Radiological Comparison of Focal Nodular Hyperplasia and Fibrolamellar Carcinoma: Feature FNH FLC Ultrasound It is difficult to detect as it has similar reflectivity to the liver. Solid, hyperechoic lesions, central scar and calcification may be seen CT Well-defined lobulated mass, isoattenuating to liver parenchyma; marked homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase with a central low-attenuation scar, mass effect visible. (Option C) Well-defined mass, often hyperattenuating; may enhance the arterial phase (Option D ruled out) MRI Isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2; central scar hypointense on T1 Hyperintense on T1 if fat-containing, significant enhancement on arterial phase. Key Differentiator Central stellate scar: Enhances on CT/MRI; no calcification Scar+ , calcification more common Hepatic adenoma (Option A) : This is usually a hypervascular lesion without a central scar or calcifications. questions.solution:
Correct answer: A. A is correct. Primary prevention aims to prevent disease onset; vaccination is a standard example. Procedure Ensure the child is standing straight with their left arm free of clothing. The arm should be bent at a right angle. Measure the distance between the tip of the shoulder (acromion) and the tip of the elbow (olecranon). Mark the midpoint on the upper arm. (Option A) The child's arm should hang relaxed by their side, with the palm facing the thigh. Use a MUAC tape to wrap around the marked midpoint of the arm. The tape should be snug but not tight enough to pinch the skin. Record the measurement at the zero mark of the tape. questions.solutionHtml:
> 

MID UPPER ARM CIRCUMFERENCE (MUAC)

Definition
  • MUAC - used to assess the nutritional status of children aged 6 months to 5 years. (Option B)
  • In infants under 6 months old, the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is not utilised as a measurement criterion.

Procedure
  • Ensure the child is standing straight with their left arm free of clothing. The arm should be bent at a right angle.
  • Measure the distance between the tip of the shoulder (acromion) and the tip of the elbow (olecranon). Mark the midpoint on the upper arm. (Option A)
  • The child's arm should hang relaxed by their side, with the palm facing the thigh.
  • Use a MUAC tape to wrap around the marked midpoint of the arm. The tape should be snug but not tight enough to pinch the skin.
  • Record the measurement at the zero mark of the tape.

Shakir’s Tape

The tape is marked with different zones that correspond to various levels of malnutrition:

  • Red Zone: Indicates severe malnutrition (MUAC < 11.5 cm).
  • Yellow Zone: Indicates moderate malnutrition (MUAC between 11.5 cm and 12.5 cm). (Option C)
  • Green Zone: Indicates healthy nutritional status (MUAC > 12.5 cm) (Option D)
 

SHAKIR’S TAPE

questions.stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman presents at 30 weeks of gestation with BP of 170/110 mmHg and proteinuria. She is stable without evidence of end-organ damage. According to the algorithm for managing severe preeclampsia, what is the recommended management approach?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old pregnant woman presents at 30 weeks of gestation with BP of 170/110 mmHg and proteinuria. She is stable without evidence of end-organ damage. According to the algorithm for managing severe preeclampsia, what is the recommended management approach?

options.label: B
options.text: Consider expectant management in a tertiary care centre

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor closely for 24 hours and discharge

options.label: D
options.text: Administer antenatal corticosteroids and terminate pregnancy

questions.answerText: Consider expectant management in a tertiary care centre
questions.solution: > Before 34 weeks of gestation with severe hypertension (BP > 160/110mm Hg), expectant management may prolong pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes if maternal and fetal conditions are stable. Algorithm for Treating Preeclampsia Initial Evaluation Perform comprehensive maternal and fetal evaluation. CBC with platelet estimate, serum creatinine, LDH, AST, ALT, and proteinuria testing. Fetal evaluation: USG for estimated fetal weight, amniotic fluid volume, and fetal antepartum testing. Decision for Delivery vs Expectant Management 34+ Weeks Gestation: Deliver promptly upon maternal stabilization or with labor/prelabor rupture of membranes; do not delay for steroid administration. Before 34 Weeks Gestation with Severe Preeclampsia: Consider expectant management in a tertiary care setting if maternal and fetal conditions are stable. 37+ Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Opt for delivery rather than expectant management upon diagnosis. Before 37 Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Managed as an outpatient; requires frequent fetal and maternal evaluation. Deliver only if specific conditions necessitate immediate intervention. Management During Expectant Management Closely monitor maternal and fetal conditions. Serial laboratory testing: CBC, liver enzymes, serum creatinine. Use antihypertensive therapy for acute-onset severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg). Administer antenatal corticosteroids and monitor for 48 hours if delivery is indicated before 34 weeks gestation. Regularly check for Conditions Necessitating Delivery Regardless of Gestational Age Maternal Conditions Fetal Conditions HELLP syndrome Pulmonary edema Eclampsia Suspected acute placental abruption, or vaginal bleeding without placenta previa Uncontrolled severe-range blood pressure Worsening renal function Persistent headaches, epigastric/right upper quadrant pain Visual disturbances Motor deficits Altered sensorium Stroke Myocardial infarction Abnormal fetal testing Fetal death Fetus with low survival likelihood (lethal anomaly, Extreme prematurity) Persistent reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery Postpartum Management Monitor blood pressure and symptoms post-delivery. Consider NSAIDs for pain management instead of opioids. Delivery is typically done at or after 34 weeks of gestation, not necessarily at 30 weeks without severe features ( Option A ruled out) . Monitoring for fetal distress is part of ongoing management, not initial for severe preeclampsia without immediate delivery indications ( Option C ruled out) Corticosteroids are recommended if delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks also no need to terminate the pregnancy (Option D ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Before 34 weeks of gestation with severe hypertension (BP > 160/110mm Hg), expectant management may prolong pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes if maternal and fetal conditions are stable.

 

Algorithm for Treating Preeclampsia

Initial Evaluation
  • Perform comprehensive maternal and fetal evaluation.
  • CBC with platelet estimate, serum creatinine, LDH, AST, ALT, and proteinuria testing.
  • Fetal evaluation: USG for estimated fetal weight, amniotic fluid volume, and fetal antepartum testing.

Decision for Delivery vs Expectant Management
  • 34+ Weeks Gestation: Deliver promptly upon maternal stabilization or with labor/prelabor rupture of membranes; do not delay for steroid administration.
  • Before 34 Weeks Gestation with Severe Preeclampsia: Consider expectant management in a tertiary care setting if maternal and fetal conditions are stable.
  • 37+ Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Opt for delivery rather than expectant management upon diagnosis.
  • Before 37 Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Managed as an outpatient; requires frequent fetal and maternal evaluation. Deliver only if specific conditions necessitate immediate intervention.

Management During Expectant Management
  • Closely monitor maternal and fetal conditions.
  • Serial laboratory testing: CBC, liver enzymes, serum creatinine.
  • Use antihypertensive therapy for acute-onset severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg).
  • Administer antenatal corticosteroids and monitor for 48 hours if delivery is indicated before 34 weeks gestation. 

Regularly check for Conditions Necessitating Delivery Regardless of Gestational Age

Maternal Conditions

Fetal Conditions
  • HELLP syndrome
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Eclampsia
  • Suspected acute placental abruption, or vaginal bleeding without placenta previa
  • Uncontrolled severe-range blood pressure
  • Worsening renal function
  • Persistent headaches, epigastric/right upper quadrant pain
  • Visual disturbances
  • Motor deficits
  • Altered sensorium
  • Stroke
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Abnormal fetal testing
  • Fetal death
  • Fetus with low survival likelihood (lethal anomaly, Extreme prematurity)
  • Persistent reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery

Postpartum Management
  • Monitor blood pressure and symptoms post-delivery.
  • Consider NSAIDs for pain management instead of opioids.

 

Delivery is typically done at or after 34 weeks of gestation, not necessarily at 30 weeks without severe features (Option A ruled out).

 

Monitoring for fetal distress is part of ongoing management, not initial for severe preeclampsia without immediate delivery indications (Option C ruled out)

 

Corticosteroids are recommended if delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks also no need to terminate the pregnancy (Option D ruled out)

questions.solution: papules or ulcers found at the uvulopalatoglossal junction and are characteristic of Roseola infantum ( sixth disease ). They typically appear following a high fever that abruptly resolves, accompanied by the development of a rash. Roseola Infantum or Exanthem subitum or Sixth disease Causative agent: Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6B). Nearly all children are infected by age 2, and peak infection occurs between 6 and 9 months of age. Spread via saliva or respiratory droplets from asymptomatic individuals. Characterised by a sudden high fever lasting 3-5 days, followed by the abrupt onset of a maculopapular rash that begins on the trunk and spreads to the extremities. Koplik Spots (Option A) are small, bluish-white spots with a red halo located on the buccal mucosa at the level of premolars and are diagnostic for measles (Rubeola). Forchheimer spots (Option C) are small reddish spots on the soft palate or uvula, indicative of rubella (German measles). Café au Lait Spots (Option D) are light brown skin patches with irregular borders, often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ity in PCOS Letrozole (preferred over clomiphene citrate) Aromatase inhibitors No antiestrogenic action on the endometrium and cervix thus yielding better pregnancy rate. Induces Mono Follicular stimulation, thus avoiding multiple pregnancy No hyperstimulation syndrome Side effect - drowsiness Clomiphene citrate (Option B) Unlike letrozole, it has anti-estrogenic action on the endometrium and cervix, thereby decreasing the fertility rate. It can cause hyperstimulation Syndrome in <1% of patients. It induces ovulation in 80% of the cases and 40-45% conceive. Co-administration of dexamethasone leads to better outcomes. In resistant cases, Tamoxifen 80-160 mg daily for 5 days tried. Metformin It is used as an insulin sensitiser. Reduces the insulin level, delays glucose absorption and production of glucose in the liver It also improves the peripheral utilisation of the glucose. Reduces the free and total testosterone increases SHBG. Contraindicated in hepatic and renal disease Nowadays, instead of Metformin, some gynaecologists prefer using N-acetyl cysteine with micronutrients. This reduces the homocysteine level. Ketoconazole 800mg daily reduces testosterone secretion. Cyproterone acetate (Option A) is an anti-androgenic producer, which is a component of the oral contraceptive pills; no role here. questions.solutionHtml:
ity in PCOS

Letrozole (preferred over clomiphene citrate)

  • Aromatase inhibitors
  • No antiestrogenic action on the endometrium and cervix thus yielding better pregnancy rate.
  • Induces Mono Follicular stimulation, thus avoiding multiple pregnancy
  • No hyperstimulation syndrome
  • Side effect - drowsiness

Clomiphene citrate (Option B)

  • Unlike letrozole, it has anti-estrogenic action on the endometrium and cervix, thereby decreasing the fertility rate.
  • It can cause hyperstimulation Syndrome in <1% of patients.
  • It induces ovulation in 80% of the cases and 40-45% conceive.
  • Co-administration of dexamethasone leads to better outcomes.
  • In resistant cases, Tamoxifen 80-160 mg daily for 5 days tried.

Metformin

  • It is used as an insulin sensitiser.
  • Reduces the insulin level, delays glucose absorption and production of glucose in the liver
  • It also improves the peripheral utilisation of the glucose. Reduces the free and total testosterone increases SHBG.
  • Contraindicated in hepatic and renal disease

Nowadays, instead of Metformin, some gynaecologists prefer using N-acetyl cysteine with micronutrients. This reduces the homocysteine level.

Ketoconazole 800mg daily reduces testosterone secretion.

Cyproterone acetate (Option A) is an anti-androgenic producer, which is a component of the oral contraceptive pills; no role here.

Tamoxifen (Option C) is not being used anymore for ovulation induction.

Surgical management (Option D) in the form of laparoscopic ovarian drilling is done when the ovulation induction drugs are failing. But nowadays in-vitro fertilization has replaced the surgical management.

Palomo's Operation involves suprainguinal extraperitoneal ligation of the testicular vein

 

Varicocele: Dilatation and tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus of veins and testicular veins

Common Occurrence
  • More common in tall, thin young men

Causes
  • Idiopathic
  • Absence or incompetent valve at the junction of the left testicular vein and left renal vein
  • Perpendicular entry of the left testicular vein into the left renal vein
  • Left-sided renal cell carcinoma causing blockage of the left testicular vein

  • Swelling at the root of the scrotum
  • Dragging pain in the groin and scrotum
  • "Bag of worms" feeling

  • Venous Doppler of the scrotum and groin
  • Ultrasound of the abdomen to check for kidney tumors
  • Semen analysis

Treatment Options
  • Palomo's Operation: Suprainguinal extraperitoneal ligation of the testicular vein
  • Ligation of veins
  • Excision of veins

questions.solution: Proximal RTA results from a defect in bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. The patient’s symptoms and laboratory findings match those of proximal RTA, making it the most likely diagnosis. RTA Features Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 2) Caused by a defect in bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Associated with generalized proximal tubular dysfunction. Symptoms include low plasma bicarbonate, glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, hypophosphatemia, and hypokalemia The urine pH may be acidic when plasma bicarbonate is low. Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 1) Results from an inability to acidify the urine in the distal tubule. Characterized by persistently high urine pH (>5.5), hypokalemia, and a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Often associated with nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis. (Option A) Hyperkalemic Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 4) Characterized by hyperkalemia and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Common in conditions such as diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. (Option C) D) While CKD can lead to metabolic acidosis, it typically presents with features such as elevated serum creatinine and urea levels and a mixed acid-base disturbance that may include both metabolic acidosis and changes in electrolyte balance. The patient's specific findings are more indicative of proximal RTA rather than CKD alone. @Neet_pg_bot

RTA

Features

Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 2)
  • Caused by a defect in bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
  • Associated with generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.
  • Symptoms include low plasma bicarbonate, glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, hypophosphatemia, and hypokalemia
  • The urine pH may be acidic when plasma bicarbonate is low.

Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 1)
  • Results from an inability to acidify the urine in the distal tubule.
  • Characterized by persistently high urine pH (>5.5), hypokalemia, and a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis.
  • Often associated with nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis. (Option A)

Hyperkalemic Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type 4)
  • Characterized by hyperkalemia and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis.
  • Common in conditions such as diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. (Option C)

 

D) While CKD can lead to metabolic acidosis, it typically presents with features such as elevated serum creatinine and urea levels and a mixed acid-base disturbance that may include both metabolic acidosis and changes in electrolyte balance. The patient's specific findings are more indicative of proximal RTA rather than CKD alone.

questions.solution: suggestive of tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose , especially given the history of suicidal behavior . Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment of choice for TCA toxicity , particularly in patients with cardiovascular instability or QRS widening on ECG. It works by: Alkalinizing the serum , which reduces TCA binding to sodium channels. Increasing plasma protein binding of TCAs, thereby reducing free drug levels. Counteracting metabolic acidosis . Naloxone (Option D): Incorrect because opioid overdose presents with pinpoint pupils , respiratory depression, and unconsciousness. Anterior Uveitis

Examination Findings:

    •

  • Muddy Iris:

  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:

    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

Koeppe's Nodules

 

 

Herpes Simplex Keratitis (Option A):

Conjunctivitis (Option B):

  • Does not cause keratic precipitates , hazy anterior chamber and a constricted pupil.

cularly in unvaccinated individuals, treatment requires thorough wound cleaning, a full series of rabies vaccinations, and Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) around the wound to provide immediate passive immunity.

Category

Exposure Type

Management

Category I

  • Touching or feeding animals

  • Licking of intact skin

  • Ensure proper hygiene

  • No treatment required

  • Minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding

    • Human rabies Immunoglobulin or HRIG

eta" data-dictid="59ff8b38191692777201150e72ebc3">uterine filling and bilateral patent tubes.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG):

  • Visualising the uterine cavity & fallopian tubes by retrograde injection of radiocontrast dye to identify filling defects & blocks.
  • Timing of HSG: 
    • postmenstrual period
    • follicular phase 
    • usually D6-D11 of mesntrual cycle to avoid it during pregnancy and ensure endomtrium is thin for better visualisation

Preparation
  • NSAID 30 minutes before to prevent tubal spasm.
  • Paracervical block in patients with cervical stenosis.

4 phases of radiographic images taken
  • Pre-contrast preliminary.
  • During contrast filling.
  • Contrast spillage into the peritoneum.
  • During deflation and withdrawal.

Contraindications
  • Acute pelvic infections.
  • Active uterine bleeding.
  • Allergic to iodine.
  • Pregnancy.

Doxycycline can be given
  • If dilated tubes are identified (indicating previous pelvic infection).
  • As prophylaxis to prevent infections post-HSG.

Complications
  • Pelvic discomfort.
  • Uterine perforation.
  • Vasovagal reactions.
  • Dye allergy.
  • Intravascular dissemination of the dye.

Saline infusion sonography (Option A) or sonosalpingography uses ultrasound to visualise the uterus & tubes while simultaneously injecting saline (not radiocontrast dye) retrograde into the uterus.

Sonoelastography (Option C) is used to assess soft tissue stiffness.

questions.solution: p> Migrating Motor Complex (MMC): Cyclic, recurring motility pattern occurs in the stomach and small intestine during fasting between meals. The MMC occurs during fasting periods between digestion, not during active digestion. Its primary role is to clear the stomach and small intestine of luminal contents in preparation for the next meal rather than facilitating nutrient absorption. The hormone motilin initiates the MMC. questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a history of self-harm, chronic emptiness, and unstable relationships often alternates between idealizing and devaluing others. What defense mechanism is most commonly observed in this disorder?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with a history of self-harm, chronic emptiness, and unstable relationships often alternates between idealizing and devaluing others. What defense mechanism is most commonly observed in this disorder?
questions.solution: nation: Splitting is a common defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder, where individuals view people or situations as either all good or all bad, contributing to their unstable relationships. BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER: General Characteristics More common in females than in males. Persons with BPD are often in a state of crisis, with frequent mood swings, shifting from being argumentative to depressed, and later feeling numb. They can experience short-lived psychotic episodes and their behavior is highly unpredictable, Self-Destructive Behaviors Repetitive self-destructive acts such as wrist slashing or self-mutilation, often to elicit help from others, express anger, or numb overwhelming emotions. Interpersonal Relationships Individuals with BPD have tumultuous interpersonal relationships, feeling both dependent on others and hostile toward them when frustrated. They cannot tolerate being alone and prefer companionship, even in unhealthy relationships. Identity and Emotional Experience Chronic feelings of emptiness, boredom, and a lack of a consistent sense of identity (identity diffusion) are common, with some complaining of feeling depressed despite fluctuating moods. Distorted Relationships Relationships are distorted, with others seen as either "all good" or "all bad" due to splitting , leading to idealization or devaluation of people. Defense Mechanism Projective identification is a common defense mechanism, where patients project unacceptable aspects of themselves onto others, inducing them to play the projected role. Treatment Dialectical behaviour therapy. Mentalization based therapy. Transference: Focussed Psychotherapy. Pharmacotherapy: Antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers like carbamazepine. Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where individuals redirect unacceptable impulses or emotions into socially acceptable behaviors or activities. Rationalization (Option C) involves explaining away or justifying behaviors or feelings to make them seem more acceptable or less distressing. Displacement (Option D) involves shifting emotions from a threatening target to a safer one, such as expressing anger toward a friend instead of an authority figure. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
nation:
  • Splitting is a common defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder, where individuals view people or situations as either all good or all bad, contributing to their unstable relationships.

 

BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER:

 

General Characteristics

  • More common in females than in males.
  • Persons with BPD are often in a state of crisis, with frequent mood swings, shifting from being argumentative to depressed, and later feeling numb.
  • They can experience short-lived psychotic episodes and their behavior is highly unpredictable,

 

Self-Destructive Behaviors

  • Repetitive self-destructive acts such as wrist slashing or self-mutilation, often to elicit help from others, express anger, or numb overwhelming emotions.

 

Interpersonal Relationships

  • Individuals with BPD have tumultuous interpersonal relationships, feeling both dependent on others and hostile toward them when frustrated.
  • They cannot tolerate being alone and prefer companionship, even in unhealthy relationships.

 

Identity and Emotional Experience

  • Chronic feelings of emptiness, boredom, and a lack of a consistent sense of identity (identity diffusion) are common, with some complaining of feeling depressed despite fluctuating moods.

 

Distorted Relationships

  • Relationships are distorted, with others seen as either "all good" or "all bad" due to splitting, leading to idealization or devaluation of people.

 

Defense Mechanism

  • Projective identification is a common defense mechanism, where patients project unacceptable aspects of themselves onto others, inducing them to play the projected role.

 

Treatment

  • Dialectical behaviour therapy.
  • Mentalization based therapy.
  • Transference: Focussed Psychotherapy.
  • Pharmacotherapy: Antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers like carbamazepine.

 

Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where individuals redirect unacceptable impulses or emotions into socially acceptable behaviors or activities.

Rationalization (Option C) involves explaining away or justifying behaviors or feelings to make them seem more acceptable or less distressing.

Displacement (Option D) involves shifting emotions from a threatening target to a safer one, such as expressing anger toward a friend instead of an authority figure.

questions.stem: A scientist observes the process of DNA replication in a human stem cell. He takes a sample of double-stranded DNA from the cell and studies it separately. He finds that the total amount of adenine in the sample is 24%. From the given information, what percentage of cytosine is present in the sample?
questions.stemHtml: A scientist observes the process of DNA replication in a human stem cell. He takes a sample of double-stranded DNA from the cell and studies it separately. He finds that the total amount of adenine in the sample is 24%. From the given information, what percentage of cytosine is present in the sample?
questions.solution: According to Chargaff’s Rule , DNA follows base-pairing where: Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T) Cytosine (C) pairs with Guanine (G) Given Adenine (A) = 24% , this means Thymine (T) = 24% as well. The total percentage of A + T = 24% + 24% = 48% . Since DNA is double-stranded , the remaining percentage must be from Cytosine (C) and Guanine (G) . C + G = 100% - 48% = 52% . As C and G are equal in amount , we divide: C = G = 52% ÷ 2 = 26% . . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• According to Chargaff’s Rule, DNA follows base-pairing where:
    • Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T)
    • Cytosine (C) pairs with Guanine (G)
  • Given Adenine (A) = 24%, this means Thymine (T) = 24% as well.
  • The total percentage of A + T = 24% + 24% = 48%.
  • Since DNA is double-stranded, the remaining percentage must be from Cytosine (C) and Guanine (G).
    • C + G = 100% - 48% = 52%.
    • As C and G are equal in amount, we divide:
      C = G = 52% ÷ 2 = 26%.

Dementia with Lewy Bodies

  • Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline sufficient to interfere with social or occupational functioning.
  • Early symptoms may include difficulties with attention, fronto-subcortical skills, and visuospatial ability, rather than prominent memory issues.

 

Clinical Features:

Probable DLB requires two or more core symptoms, while possible DLB requires at least one.

Core Features

Supporting Features
  • Fluctuating levels of attention and alertness (Option A ruled out)
  • Recurrent visual hallucinations (Option B ruled out)
  • Parkinsonian features (e.g., cogwheeling, bradykinesia, resting tremor) (Option D ruled out)
  • REM Sleep behavior disorder
  • Repeated falls
  • Syncope
  • Sensitivity to neuroleptics
  • Systematized delusions (Option C)
  • Hallucinations in other modalities (e.g., auditory, tactile)

 

Differences in features of LBD and PD:

Feature

Lewy Body Dementia (LBD)

Parkinson's Disease (PD)

Onset of Symptoms

Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms appear early; motor symptoms develop later.

Primarily motor symptoms appear first (e.g., bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors).

Visual Hallucinations

Common and can occur early.

Less common initially; may occur later, often due to treatment.

Fluctuations in Attention

Fluctuations in alertness and attention are characteristic.

Fluctuations are primarily related to medication cycles.

Response to Medications

Poor response to dopaminergic medications; risk of worsening psychiatric symptoms.

Generally improves with dopaminergic medications (e.g., levodopa).

Sleep Disturbances

REM sleep behavior disorder is common and can precede cognitive symptoms.

REM sleep behavior disorder may occur but is primarily linked to motor symptoms.

Progression

Rapid progression of cognitive and behavioral symptoms.

Gradual progression of motor symptoms, with cognitive decline developing later.

 

Pathology:

  • Lewy body disease presents clinically similarly to Alzheimer’s disease but is marked by hallucinations, parkinsonian features, and extrapyramidal signs.
  • Lewy bodies, which are abnormal accumulations of α-synuclein aggregates, are found in the cerebral cortex and substantia nigra.
  • In cases where Lewy body pathology coexists with Alzheimer’s, the amygdala is often the only affected region.
  • Patients with Lewy body dementia may exhibit Capgras syndrome (reduplicative paramnesia), highlighting the complex nature of their symptoms.

questions.solution: strong>Explanation: HRCT chest in an immunocompromised patient shows an air crescent sign (right lung) and Halo sign ( posterior segment of the left lower lobe, abutting the vertebral body ) seen in Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Galactomannan antigen test on BAL is a sensitive and specific biomarker for diagnosing invasive aspergillosis. It detects a polysaccharide component of the Aspergillus cell wall that is released during active infection. Beta-1,3-D-glucan is more panfungal , so it's helpful in screening but less specific. The BACTEC™ MGIT 960 system is an automated, rapid culture system used primarily for the detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria from clinical specimens. questions.solution: with Rigler's triad (small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, and ectopic gallstone) and the corresponding imaging findings, the most likely diagnosis is gallstone ileus . The optimal initial surgical management is enterolithotomy , which effectively relieves the intestinal obstruction by removing the impacted gallstone. with Rigler's triad (small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, and ectopic gallstone) and the corresponding imaging findings, the most likely diagnosis is gallstone ileus. The optimal initial surgical management is enterolithotomy, which effectively relieves the intestinal obstruction by removing the impacted gallstone.


 

Effects and Complications of Gallstones:

 

Gallbladder

Common bile duct and pancreas

Small intestine
  • Acute cholecystitis
  • Chronic cholecystitis
  • Mucocele
  • Empyema
  • Gangrene
  • Perforation
  • Carcinoma gallbladder
  • CBD stones
  • Biliary obstruction (Jaundice)
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Mirizzi syndrome

Gallstone ileus leading to intestinal obstruction

 

Gallstone Ileus

  • Acute cholecystitis→ erosion of inflamed tissues → Formation of a cholecystointestinal fistula→ Gallstone ileus
  • Small gallstones typically pass through the intestines, but stones 2–5 cm in size can become impacted, usually in the terminal ileum or at the ileocecal valve.

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Acute, intermittent, or chronic episodes of partial or complete gastrointestinal obstruction.
  • Signs of obstruction include dehydration, abdominal distension and tenderness, high-pitched bowel sounds, and obstructive jaundice.

Diagnosis:

  • Plain Abdominal Radiograph:
    • Partial or complete intestinal obstruction
    • Pneumobilia or contrast material in the biliary tree
    • Calcified gallstone with position changes on serial films (tumbling sign)
  • CT Scan:
    • Superior sensitivity (up to 93%)
    • Shows abnormal gallbladder with air, air-fluid level, or fluid accumulation with an irregular wall

Management:

  • Management of intestinal obstruction
  • Enterolithotomy: The most common surgical procedure
    • A longitudinal incision on the antimesenteric border proximal to the site of impaction
    • Gallstone is brought to a non-edematous bowel segment by gentle manipulation and extraction.
  • Cholecystoenteric fistula resection only if the patient is stable and there are residual gallstones that may cause infection or recurrent ileus

Cholecystectomy and fistula repair (Option A): While important, this is not the initial step due to the patient's unstable condition and intestinal obstruction.

Endoscopic removal of the gallstone (Option B): Not feasible for this condition due to the intestinal obstruction.

complication specific to monochorionic twins (not DCDA) due to sharing of placenta & in those with problematic deep arterio-venous connections between the placentas. Such connections are more often encountered in MCDA twins rather than MCMA twins.

Maternal Complications can be divided into 3 stages:

  • Pregnancy
  • Labor
  • Puerperium

 

Pregnancy

Labor

Puerperium
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Anemia
  • PIH and pre-eclampsia
  • Polyhydramnios/ oligohydramnios

  • Malpresentation

  • Operative interference
  • Postpartum hemorrhage
  • Subinvolution
  • Infection

Preterm labor (Option B ) occurs frequently (in 50% of cases) in twin pregnancies, with twins typically being delivered around 37 weeks gestation on average. The causes include excessive stretching of the uterus, increased amniotic fluid (hydramnios), and premature rupture of membranes

 

Pre-eclampsia (Option C): The risk is three times higher in twin pregnancies, possibly due to increased exposure to an excess of chorionic villi 

 

Malpresentation (Option D) is more frequent in twins compared to single pregnancies. Approximately 70% of the time, the first baby presents headfirst (vertex), and in 50% of cases, both babies present headfirst. Therefore, malpresentation is more commonly observed in the second baby

An image of the X-ray of the left knee joint is shown below. What is Phemister’s triad, and how does it relate to this case?

options.label: B

options.label: C

Explanation: Phemister’s triad of juxta-articular osteopenia/osteoporosis, peripheral osseous erosions, and joint space narrowing suggests tuberculous arthritis but is nonspecific.

X-ray findings:

  • Characteristic signs are soft-tissue swelling and periarticular osteoporosis.
  • Bone ends appear ‘washed-out,’ and the articular space narrows.
  • In children, epiphyses may enlarge due to prolonged hyperemia.
  • Subarticular bone erosion occurs on both sides, indicating synovial inflammation.
  • Cystic lesions may appear in adjacent bone ends.
  • Little to no periosteal reaction, unlike a pyogenic infection, where reactive periosteal new bone formation is an important feature.
  • Phemister’s triad of juxta-articular osteopenia/osteoporosis, peripheral osseous erosions, and joint space narrowing suggests tuberculous arthritis but is nonspecific. (Option B)

 

A triad of symptoms indicating septic arthritis (Option A): Septic arthritis typically presents with sudden onset of joint pain, swelling, and fever, often with systemic signs of infection. The radiological findings associated with septic arthritis usually include joint effusion, slight subluxation, and periosteal reaction but do not specifically include Phemister’s triad. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

A set of criteria for diagnosing osteosarcoma (Option C): Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer that typically presents with bone pain particularly at night, and swelling, and may have characteristic radiological features like a sunburst pattern or Codman's triangle. However, it is not related to Phemister’s triad. Thus, this option is incorrect.

A triad of radiological criteria for diagnosing Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Option D): It is a chronic inflammatory condition in children that can present with joint pain, swelling, and systemic symptoms like fever. The radiological findings are synovial thickening, joint effusion, cartilage loss, and bone erosions. Phemister’s triad is not a feature of JIA. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

questions.stem: A physician receives a court notice asking him to appear in court to testify in a malpractice case. The notice explicitly orders him to bring relevant patient records to support his testimony. However, he failed to attend court on the scheduled date and did not submit any reason for his absence. Based on the nature of the notice he received and the legal implications of missing the court date, what type of court order did he receive, and what could be the potential legal consequence of his failure to comply?
questions.stemHtml: A physician receives a court notice asking him to appear in court to testify in a malpractice case. The notice explicitly orders him to bring relevant patient records to support his testimony. However, he failed to attend court on the scheduled date and did not submit any reason for his absence. Based on the nature of the notice he received and the legal implications of missing the court date, what type of court order did he receive, and what could be the potential legal consequence of his failure to comply?

options.label: A
options.text: Subpoena ad testificandum, with a fine and/or imprisonment for contempt of court

options.label: B
options.text: Subpoena ad testificandum, with a warning but no legal consequences

options.label: C
options.text: Subpoena duces tecum, with the possibility of a fine and/or imprisonment for contempt

options.label: D
options.text: Subpoena duces tecum, leading to the revocation of his professional license

questions.answerText: Subpoena duces tecum, with the possibility of a fine and/or imprisonment for contempt
questions.solution: Explanation: Summons/Subpoena: A subpoena is a legal order mandating a witness to appear before a court on a specific date, time, and location to provide testimony or evidence, under penalty. A subpoena is issued by the court in writing, signed by the presiding officer, and carries the court's official seal (Sec. 63 BNSS) . Delivered to the witness by a police officer, court official, or public servant. The witness must sign and return a duplicate copy of the subpoena to acknowledge receipt (Sec. 64 BNSS). Types of Subpoenas Subpoena duces tecum (Options C and D) : The witness is required to bring specific documents or items to the court (e.g., medico-legal reports or postmortem findings). For expert witness. Subpoena ad testificandum (Options A and B) : The witness is required to appear in court to provide oral testimony. For common witnesses. Punishment for Failing to Comply with a Subpoena/Summons: 1. Civil Cases: The witness may be ordered to pay damages for failing to attend court. This involves compensation for the inconvenience caused to the parties involved in the case. 2. Criminal Cases: If a witness fails to appear in court without a justified reason, the following actions can be taken: Under 63 – 71 BNSS , the court may issue a notice to the witness to explain their absence. The court may issue notice under Section 389, BNSS and after hearing the witness, if it finds that the witness neglected to attend the court without a justified reason, may punish him under Section 208 and 209, BNS , and sentence him/her to: A fine (Rs.1000/-), OR Imprisonment (6 months), OR Both fine and imprisonment. Also, the Court may issue bailable or non-bailable warrants to secure the presence of the witness ( S.206 to 209, BNS and S.90, BNSS ). Prioritization of Summons: Criminal vs. Civil Courts : If a witness is summoned by both criminal and civil courts for the same day, they must attend the criminal court , which takes precedence. Higher vs. Lower Courts : When summoned by two courts of the same jurisdiction (e.g., civil or criminal), the witness must attend the higher court first. Multiple Summons : If the witness receives multiple summonses from the same type of court, they should attend the court that issued the first summons and notify the other. Subpoena ad testificandum, with a fine and/or imprisonment for contempt of court (Option A): Failure to attend court after receiving a Subpoena ad testificandum can result in penalties for contempt of court, including fines or imprisonment. However, it does not relate to document production, which makes it less relevant to the case scenario where documents were requested. Subpoena ad testificandum, with a warning but no legal consequences (Option B): A subpoena ad testificandum does require court attendance for testimony. However, failure to comply with any subpoena typically results in penalties, not merely a warning. Subpoena duces tecum, leading to the revocation of his professional license (Option D) : Revocation of a professional license is not a standard or direct consequence of failing to comply with a subpoena. It is unlikely unless professional misconduct is also involved. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

Summons/Subpoena:

  • A subpoena is a legal order mandating a witness to appear before a court on a specific date, time, and location to provide testimony or evidence, under penalty.
  • A subpoena is issued by the court in writing, signed by the presiding officer, and carries the court's official seal (Sec. 63 BNSS).
  • Delivered to the witness by a police officer, court official, or public servant.
  • The witness must sign and return a duplicate copy of the subpoena to acknowledge receipt (Sec. 64 BNSS).

 

Types of Subpoenas

  1. Subpoena duces tecum (Options C and D):
    • The witness is required to bring specific documents or items to the court (e.g., medico-legal reports or postmortem findings).
    • For expert witness.
  2. Subpoena ad testificandum (Options A and B):
    • The witness is required to appear in court to provide oral testimony.
    • For common witnesses.

 

Punishment for Failing to Comply with a Subpoena/Summons:

1. Civil Cases:

  • The witness may be ordered to pay damages for failing to attend court.
  • This involves compensation for the inconvenience caused to the parties involved in the case.

2. Criminal Cases:

  • If a witness fails to appear in court without a justified reason, the following actions can be taken:
  • Under 63 – 71 BNSS, the court may issue a notice to the witness to explain their absence.
  • The court may issue notice under Section 389, BNSS and after hearing the witness, if it finds that the witness neglected to attend the court without a justified reason, may punish him under Section 208 and 209, BNS, and sentence him/her to:
    • A fine (Rs.1000/-), OR
    • Imprisonment (6 months), OR
    • Both fine and imprisonment.
  • Also, the Court may issue bailable or non-bailable warrants to secure the presence of the witness (S.206 to 209, BNS and S.90, BNSS).

 

Prioritization of Summons:

  • Criminal vs. Civil Courts: If a witness is summoned by both criminal and civil courts for the same day, they must attend the criminal court, which takes precedence.
  • Higher vs. Lower Courts: When summoned by two courts of the same jurisdiction (e.g., civil or criminal), the witness must attend the higher court first.
  • Multiple Summons: If the witness receives multiple summonses from the same type of court, they should attend the court that issued the first summons and notify the other.

 

Subpoena ad testificandum, with a fine and/or imprisonment for contempt of court (Option A):

  • Failure to attend court after receiving a Subpoena ad testificandum can result in penalties for contempt of court, including fines or imprisonment.
  • However, it does not relate to document production, which makes it less relevant to the case scenario where documents were requested.

 

Subpoena ad testificandum, with a warning but no legal consequences (Option B):

  • A subpoena ad testificandum does require court attendance for testimony.
  • However, failure to comply with any subpoena typically results in penalties, not merely a warning.


Subpoena duces tecum, leading to the revocation of his professional license (Option D) :

  • Revocation of a professional license is not a standard or direct consequence of failing to comply with a subpoena.
  • It is unlikely unless professional misconduct is also involved.

questions.answerText: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa
questions.solution: osa Explanation: Urethroplasty (Surgical excision and reconstruction) is the gold standard for managing long strictures (greater than 2 cm). This surgical procedure involves removing the affected stricture segment and reconstructing the urethra using a graft taken from the buccal mucosa. Urethral Stricture Definition Abnormal narrowing of the urethra, causing partial or complete obstruction of urine flow, leading to discomfort and severe complications if untreated. Causes Trauma (Most common): Pelvic fractures, falls, accidents, or iatrogenic trauma from prolonged catheterization. Infections: STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia causing urethritis. Medical Procedures : Urethral surgeries or radiation for pelvic cancers. Inflammatory Conditions: Chronic inflammation from conditions like lichen sclerosus. Investigations Posterior Urethral Stricture: Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder during voiding. {{caption_text}} Anterior Urethral Stricture: Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU). {{caption_text}} Emergency Evaluation: Both RGU and MCU may be used in trauma cases or acute urinary retention. Management Urethral Dilation: Temporary relief with dilators, often leading to recurrence. (Option A) Optical Internal Urethrotomy (OIU): Endoscopic incision at the 12 o'clock position; effective for short bulbar strictures (<2 cm). (Option B) Urethroplasty: Surgical excision and reconstruction; the gold standard for recurrent or complex strictures (Option C) . Strictures up to 2 cm: Excision with end-to-end anastomosis. Strictures >2 cm: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa, bladder mucosa, or penile skin. Urethral Stenting (Option D) involves placing a stent in the urethra to keep it open. While stenting can relieve obstruction temporarily, it is not a definitive treatment for strictures and may be associated with complications, such as infection and migration of the stent. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

 

  • Urethroplasty (Surgical excision and reconstruction) is the gold standard for managing long strictures (greater than 2 cm).
  • This surgical procedure involves removing the affected stricture segment and reconstructing the urethra using a graft taken from the buccal mucosa.

 

Urethral Stricture

 

Definition

Abnormal narrowing of the urethra, causing partial or complete obstruction of urine flow, leading to discomfort and severe complications if untreated.

Causes

Trauma (Most common): Pelvic fractures, falls, accidents, or iatrogenic trauma from prolonged catheterization.

Infections: STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia causing urethritis.

Medical Procedures: Urethral surgeries or radiation for pelvic cancers.

Inflammatory Conditions: Chronic inflammation from conditions like lichen sclerosus.

Investigations

Posterior Urethral Stricture: Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder during voiding.

Anterior Urethral Stricture: Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU).


Emergency Evaluation: Both RGU and MCU may be used in trauma cases or acute urinary retention.

Management

Urethral Dilation: Temporary relief with dilators, often leading to recurrence. (Option A)

Optical Internal Urethrotomy (OIU): Endoscopic incision at the 12 o'clock position; effective for short bulbar strictures (<2 cm).(Option B)

Urethroplasty: Surgical excision and reconstruction; the gold standard for recurrent or complex strictures (Option C).

  • Strictures up to 2 cm: Excision with end-to-end anastomosis.
  • Strictures >2 cm: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa, bladder mucosa, or penile skin.

 

  • Urethral Stenting (Option D) involves placing a stent in the urethra to keep it open.
    • While stenting can relieve obstruction temporarily, it is not a definitive treatment for strictures and may be associated with complications, such as infection and migration of the stent.

Intravenous Regional Anesthesia (IVRA): Intravenous Regional Anesthesia (IVRA), also known as a Bier block, is a technique that provides local anesthesia to a specific region of the body, typically an extremity, through intravenous administration of a local anesthetic.

 

Indications
  • Suitable for minor surgical procedures on the upper or lower extremities (hand surgeries, forearm procedures, and foot surgeries).
  • Used when general anesthesia is not necessary and for patients with contraindications to other forms of anesthesia.

Anesthetic Agents
  • Commonly used local anesthetics include lidocaine (most frequent) and prilocaine.

Procedure Steps
  • Tourniquet Application: Apply a tourniquet to the proximal part of the extremity to prevent blood flow and keep the local anesthetic localized.
  • Venous Access: Establish intravenous access in the selected limb.
  • Administration of Anesthetic agent: Inject the local anesthetic into the IV line, typically in a volume of 40-50 mL.

Tourniquet Management

  • The tourniquet should be inflated to a pressure that is approximately 50 mmHg above systolic blood pressure.
  • It is typically safe to keep the tourniquet inflated for 30-60 minutes; prolonged inflation can increase the risk of complications.

Advantages
  • Provides effective analgesia with minimal systemic absorption.
  • Allows for a bloodless surgical field.
  • Quick onset of action and ease of administration.

Disadvantages and Complications
  • Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) Can occur if the local anesthetic enters the systemic circulation.
  • Tourniquet Pain
  • Nerve Damage

Contraindications
  • Infection at the injection site or over the tourniquet.
  • Severe peripheral vascular disease.
  • Patient refusal or inability to cooperate.

Lipid Emulsion Therapy
  • Used as a treatment for Local anesthesia systemic toxicity, acts by sequestering the local anesthetic from circulation and mitigating toxic effects.
  • Administer a 20% lipid emulsion intravenously if toxicity occurs.

questions.solution: ssociated with rickets include craniotabes, bossing of the skull, Harrison’s sulcus, and widening of wrists, all of which indicate abnormal bone development and mineralization due to vitamin D deficiency or other underlying issues related to the condition. Clinical Features of Rickets Nutritional rickets typically occurs in children around 1 year old but can also affect older children with malabsorption syndromes. The following are the clinical features: Craniotabes : This is a sign of rickets seen in young infants, where applying pressure to the soft membranous bones of the skull creates a sensation similar to compressing and releasing a ping pong ball. (Statement 1) Bossing of the Skull: Noticeable swelling of the frontal and parietal bones appears after 6 months of age. (Statement 3) Broadening of Long Bone Ends: This occurs around 6-9 months of age, most prominently at the wrists and knees. (Statement 7) Widening of wrist joint Delayed Tooth Eruption: Infants may show delays in the appearance of their teeth. Harrison's Sulcus: A horizontal depression develops along the lower part of the chest, corresponding to the diaphragm's insertion. (Statement 4) Pigeon Chest: The sternum becomes prominent. Rachitic Rosary: The junctions between the ribs and cartilage in the anterior chest wall become prominent, resembling a rosary. Muscular Hypotonia: The child may have a protruding abdomen (pot belly) due to marked muscle weakness, along with visceroptosis and lumbar lordosis. Deformities: As the child begins to walk, common presentations of rickets include deformities of the long bones, leading to knock knees or bow legs . Scorbutic rosary (Statement 2) and Perifollicular haemorrhage (Statement 5) are features associated with vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) and not rickets. Brown's tumour (Statement 6) is a feature of hyperparathyroidism and is not associated with rickets. @Neet_pg_bot

ssociated with rickets include craniotabes, bossing of the skull, Harrison’s sulcus, and widening of wrists, all of which indicate abnormal bone development and mineralization due to vitamin D deficiency or other underlying issues related to the condition.

 

Clinical Features of Rickets

Nutritional rickets typically occurs in children around 1 year old but can also affect older children with malabsorption syndromes. The following are the clinical features:

  • Craniotabes: This is a sign of rickets seen in young infants, where applying pressure to the soft membranous bones of the skull creates a sensation similar to compressing and releasing a ping pong ball. (Statement 1)
  • Bossing of the Skull: Noticeable swelling of the frontal and parietal bones appears after 6 months of age. (Statement 3)
  • Broadening of Long Bone Ends: This occurs around 6-9 months of age, most prominently at the wrists and knees. (Statement 7)

Widening of wrist joint

  • Delayed Tooth Eruption: Infants may show delays in the appearance of their teeth.
  • Harrison's Sulcus: A horizontal depression develops along the lower part of the chest, corresponding to the diaphragm's insertion. (Statement 4)

  • Pigeon Chest: The sternum becomes prominent.

  • Rachitic Rosary: The junctions between the ribs and cartilage in the anterior chest wall become prominent, resembling a rosary.
  • Muscular Hypotonia: The child may have a protruding abdomen (pot belly) due to marked muscle weakness, along with visceroptosis and lumbar lordosis.
  • Deformities: As the child begins to walk, common presentations of rickets include deformities of the long bones, leading to knock knees or bow legs.

Scorbutic rosary (Statement 2) and Perifollicular haemorrhage (Statement 5) are features associated with vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) and not rickets.

Brown's tumour (Statement 6) is a feature of hyperparathyroidism and is not associated with rickets.

Laboratory tests reveal elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 50 year old woman presents with complaints of persistent fatigue, itching, and mild right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she has jaundice and hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Explanation: The patient's symptoms, including fatigue, itching, jaundice, and hepatomegaly, along with elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies, are characteristic of primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) . PBC is an autoimmune disorder leading to the gradual destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, resulting in cholestasis and liver damage. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (Option A) also presents with cholestasis but is more often associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). PSC involves both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, which would typically be identified in imaging studies. This patient has no history of IBD, and the presentation and test results align more closely with PBC. Autoimmune hepatitis (Option C) is characterized by elevated serum transaminases rather than an isolated elevation in alkaline phosphatase. It is not commonly associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies. While drug-induced liver disease (Option D) can cause cholestasis and elevated liver enzymes, the presence of specific antibodies (AMA), the chronic nature of the patient's symptoms and the absence of drug history are more indicative of an autoimmune process like PBC . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
an> of lost significant object

Explanation:

The introjection of lost objects is a part of the psychodynamic theory of depression, while the cognitive triad is a component of the cognitive theory, involving self-perception, environment, and the future.

Psychosocial Theories of Depression

Life Events and Environmental Stress

  • Stressful life events often precede the first episode of mood disorders.
  • Initial stress may lead to long-lasting biological changes, increasing the risk for future episodes even without further stressors.

 

Psychodynamic Theories

  • Early disturbances in the infant-mother relationship predispose to depression.
  • Depression is linked to real or imagined loss of significant objects.
  • Introjection of lost objects serves as a defense mechanism.
  • Feelings of love and hate toward the lost object result in self-directed anger.

 

Cognitive Theory

  • Depression arises from cognitive distortions known as depressogenic schemata.
  • Cognitive Triad (by Aaron Beck):
    • Worthlessness: Negative self-perception. (Option A)
    • Helplessness: Perception of the environment as hostile and demanding. (Option B)
    • Hopelessness: Expectation of suffering and failure in the future. (Option C)
  • Therapy focuses on modifying these cognitive distortions.

 

Learned Helplessness

  • Developed from studies showing that exposure to uncontrollable stressors (e.g., electric shocks in dogs) leads to passive behavior.
  • Humans may internalize helplessness and lose self-esteem after adverse events.
  • Improvement in depression involves learning a sense of control and mastery over one’s environment.

 

Evolutionary Theory

  • Depression is viewed as an adaptive response to perceived environmental threats.
  • Withdrawal from social situations and decreased activity may serve as protective mechanisms.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old patient on anti-HIV therapy presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe flank pain, nausea, and vomiting. Laboratory tests reveal hematuria, and a CT scan shows evidence of nephrolithiasis. Which of the following protease inhibitors is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.solution: navir (Option A) is a protease inhibitor associated with developing nephrolithiasis (Kidney stones - Radiolucent on X-Ray / may be radiolucent on CT as well) due to its poor solubility in urine. It can lead to the formation of crystals in the urine, causing flank pain, hematuria, and potential obstruction. Indinavir also causes hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice Ritonavir (Option B): Associated with gastrointestinal disturbances, Hyperlipidemia, &Hepatotoxicity. Atazanavir (Option C): Associated with indirect hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice). Darunavir (option D): Associated with rash, liver function abnormalities, and gastrointestinal disturbances. @Neet_pg_bot

Ethambutol

MOA

Inhibits arabinosyl transferases involved in arabinogalactan synthesis, thereby interfering with mycolic acid synthesis in cell wall

Mechanism of resistance

Mutation of embAB genes, which encodes the enzyme arabinosyl transferase, reducing its affinity for ethambutol

Uses

questions.stem: A state recorded 150 maternal deaths in a year. The number of live births during the same period was 50,000. The total number of women in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) is 10,00,000. What is the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) for this state?
questions.stemHtml: A state recorded 150 maternal deaths in a year. The number of live births during the same period was 50,000. The total number of women in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) is 10,00,000. What is the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) for this state?
questions.solution: >The question specifically asks for the maternal mortality ratio. Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) is the number of maternal deaths during the antenatal period, during delivery, and up to 42 days post delivery per 100,000 live births. It is calculated as follows: Maternal Mortality Ratio = ( No. of maternal deaths / No. of Live births ) x 100000 So the answer will be, (150/50000) x 100000 = 300 @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>The question specifically asks for the maternal mortality ratio.

Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) is the number of maternal deaths during the antenatal period, during delivery, and up to 42 days post delivery per 100,000 live births. It is calculated as follows:

Maternal Mortality Ratio =  ( No. of maternal deaths / No. of Live births )    x   100000

So the answer will be, (150/50000) x 100000 = 300

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with schizophrenia, who has been stable on antipsychotics for years, was recently switched to a higher dose of a first-generation antipsychotic. He then becomes increasingly agitated, develops a high fever, and exhibits severe muscle stiffness, appearing less responsive and confused. The involved receptors and the drug of choice for managing this condition are:
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male with schizophrenia, who has been stable on antipsychotics for years, was recently switched to a higher dose of a first-generation antipsychotic. He then becomes increasingly agitated, develops a high fever, and exhibits severe muscle stiffness, appearing less responsive and confused. The involved receptors and the drug of choice for managing this condition are:
questions.solution: The scenario is indicative of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) , in which the blockage of D2 receptors leads to extrapyramidal side effects, and the drug of choice for treatment is Dantrolene sodium. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) Description A rare, potentially fatal consequence of neuroleptic administration. Mechanism D2 receptor blocking at: Striatum (muscle rigidity) Hypothalamus (hyperthermia) Spinal nerves (autonomic disturbances) Clinical manifestations Motor and behavioural Autonomic symptoms Muscular rigidity (most common) Dystonia Akinesia, Mutism Obtundation Agitation Fever (most common) Diaphoresis Raised pulse and blood pressure Sweating Altered consciousness Associated conditions Renal failure and myoglobinuria Laboratory findings Raised levels of creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) (most common) Leukocytosis (raised WBC) Raised liver enzymes Raised plasma myoglobin Management Stop the drug (causing symptoms) Supportive care (maintain hydration and other vitals) Skeletal muscle relaxants: Dantrolene sodium (drug of choice) Dopamine agonists: Bromocriptine, Amantadine Second-generation antipsychotics (for restarting the treatment for Schizophrenia). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The scenario is indicative of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), in which the blockage of D2 receptors leads to extrapyramidal side effects, and the drug of choice for treatment is Dantrolene sodium.

 

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

Description

A rare, potentially fatal consequence of neuroleptic administration.

Mechanism

D2 receptor blocking at:

  • Striatum (muscle rigidity)
  • Hypothalamus (hyperthermia)
  • Spinal nerves (autonomic disturbances)
 

Clinical manifestations

Motor and behavioural

Autonomic symptoms
  • Muscular rigidity (most common)
  • Dystonia
  • Akinesia,
  • Mutism
  • Obtundation
  • Agitation
  • Fever (most common)
  • Diaphoresis
  • Raised pulse and blood pressure
  • Sweating
  • Altered consciousness

Associated conditions

Renal failure and myoglobinuria

Laboratory findings
  • Raised levels of creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) (most common)
  • Leukocytosis (raised WBC)
  • Raised liver enzymes
  • Raised plasma myoglobin

Management

  • Stop the drug (causing symptoms)
  • Supportive care (maintain hydration and other vitals)
  • Skeletal muscle relaxants: Dantrolene sodium (drug of choice)
  • Dopamine agonists: Bromocriptine, Amantadine
  • Second-generation antipsychotics (for restarting the treatment for Schizophrenia).
