questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear. Audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, and an MRI shows no abnormalities in the cochlear nerve. A defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals is suspected. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear. Audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, and an MRI shows no abnormalities in the cochlear nerve. A defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals is suspected. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.solution: anation: The patient presents with sensorineural hearing loss, typically caused by damage to the inner ear or the neural pathways responsible for hearing. Given the defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals, the likely issue lies in the Organ of Corti, where the hair cells transduce sound vibrations into electrical impulses. The Organ of Corti , located on the basilar membrane inside the cochlea, contains the hair cells responsible for the hearing transduction mechanism . When sound waves are transmitted through the ear and reach the inner ear, they cause vibrations of the basilar membrane , which bend stereocilia on the hair cells. Inner hair cells are arranged in a single row, while outer hair cells form three to four rows. Inner hair cells transmit auditory stimuli to the brain, while outer hair cells modulate inner hair cell function to enhance sound sensitivity and clarity. This bending opens ion channels, generating electrical impulses. These impulses are sent through the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound. Oval window (Option A) is a membrane-covered opening between the middle and inner ear. It plays a role in the mechanical conduction of sound by transmitting vibrations from the stapes to the fluid in the cochlea but is in converting those vibrations into electrical signals. Tympanic membrane (Option C) vibrates in response to sound and transmits from the external ear to the ossicles of the middle ear. Damage leads to conductive hearing loss but doesn't affect sound transduction. Stapes footplate (Option D): This structure amplifies sound waves but involves the conductive hearing process, not sensorineural conversion. @Neet_pg_bot

  • When sound waves are transmitted through the ear and reach the inner ear, they cause vibrations of the basilar membrane, which bend stereocilia on the hair cells.
  • Inner hair cells are arranged in a single row, while outer hair cells form three to four rows.
  • Inner hair cells transmit auditory stimuli to the brain, while outer hair cells modulate inner hair cell function to enhance sound sensitivity and clarity.
  • This bending opens ion channels, generating electrical impulses.
  • These impulses are sent through the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound.

Oval window (Option A) is a membrane-covered opening between the middle and inner ear.

  • It plays a role in the mechanical conduction of sound by transmitting vibrations from the stapes to the fluid in the cochlea but is in converting those vibrations into electrical signals.

Tympanic membrane (Option C) vibrates in response to sound and transmits from the external ear to the ossicles of the middle ear.

  • Damage leads to conductive hearing loss but doesn't affect sound transduction.

Stapes footplate (Option D):

  • This structure amplifies sound waves but involves the conductive hearing process, not sensorineural conversion.

questions.stem: A 65 y/o male presents with persistent tearing in his right eye that has worsened over the past year. The physician orders an imaging study to pinpoint the exact location of the blockage and assess the condition of the lacrimal sac. Which investigation is most appropriate for this purpose?
questions.stemHtml: A 65 y/o male presents with persistent tearing in his right eye that has worsened over the past year. The physician orders an imaging study to pinpoint the exact location of the blockage and assess the condition of the lacrimal sac. Which investigation is most appropriate for this purpose?
questions.solution: highly detailed anatomical information about the entire lacrimal drainage system. By injecting contrast dye into the lacrimal sac and taking X-rays, DCG can precisely identify the site, extent, and nature of the blockage, making it the investigation of choice when anatomical clarity is required. Fluorescein Dye Disappearance Test (FDDT) (Option B): It is mainly used to assess the overall efficiency of tear drainage and does not provide information on the exact location or nature of any obstruction within the lacrimal system. Dacryoscintigraphy (Option C) or lacrimal scintillography is a functional test that evaluates the rate at which tears flow through the lacrimal drainage system by tracking a radioactive tracer. While it is useful for identifying functional delays or blockages, it lacks the anatomical precision needed to determine the exact location or cause of the obstruction. Lacrimal Syringing (Option D): Normal saline is injected into the lacrimal sac using a syringe. Although it can identify the degree of blockage & approximate blockage site, it does not offer detailed anatomical information. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl presents to the clinic with complaints of severe lower abdominal pain that has occurred cyclically every month for the past six months, but she has never had a menstrual period. She reports no other significant symptoms. On physical examination, her secondary sexual characteristics are well-developed (Tanner stage 4). A pelvic examination reveals a bulging, bluish membrane at the introitus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis, along with the type of amenorrhea?
questions.stemHtml:
A 14-year-old girl presents to the clinic with complaints of severe lower abdominal pain that has occurred cyclically every month for the past six months, but she has never had a menstrual period. She reports no other significant symptoms. On physical examination, her secondary sexual characteristics are well-developed (Tanner stage 4). A pelvic examination reveals a bulging, bluish membrane at the introitus.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis, along with the type of amenorrhea?
questions.solution: hymen is a common cause of primary amenorrhea with cyclic abdominal pain. A bulging, bluish membrane at the introitus is a classic sign of this condition, indicating the accumulation of menstrual blood behind the hymen. Cryptomenorrhea is a type of primary amenorrhea in which menstruation occurs but is not visible due to obstruction of the outflow tract (such as Imperforate hymen). Primary Amenorrhea is diagnosed when a young girl who has not yet menstruated by: 13 years (in the absence of secondary sexual characters). 15 years (regardless of the presence of secondary sexual characters). Causes of Primary Amenorrhea Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism Primary ovarian failure Resistant ovarian syndrome Galactosemia Developmental defect of genital tract Müllerian agenesis (2nd most common cause) Imperforate hymen (Cryptomenorrhea) Vaginal agenesis Transverse vaginal septum Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Hypothalamic and pituitary dysfunction Kallmann’s syndrome Craniopharyngioma Abnormal chromosomal pattern Turner’s syndrome (most common cause) Pure gonadal dysgenesis Androgen insensitivity syndrome Transverse Vaginal Septum - Primary Amenorrhea (Option A): On examination, the hymen would appear normal because the obstruction is higher up in the vaginal canal, not at the introitus. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS) - Primary Amenorrhea (Option C): These patients lack a uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina due to normal regression of the Müllerian structures (induced by anti-Müllerian hormone). Therefore, there would be no menstruation and no cyclic abdominal pain. Examination may reveal a short and blind ending vagina. Müllerian Agenesis - Primary Amenorrhea (Option D): Secondary sexual characteristics develop normally. However, there is an absence of the uterus, upper vagina, and fallopian tubes, so the patient would not experience cyclic abdominal pain as there is no menstruation. The examination would reveal a shortened or absent vagina, not a bluish bulging hymen. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
hymen is a common cause of primary amenorrhea with cyclic abdominal pain. A bulging, bluish membrane at the introitus is a classic sign of this condition, indicating the accumulation of menstrual blood behind the hymen.
  • Cryptomenorrhea is a type of primary amenorrhea in which menstruation occurs but is not visible due to obstruction of the outflow tract (such as Imperforate hymen).

    •  

    Primary Amenorrhea is diagnosed when a young girl who has not yet menstruated by:

    • 13 years (in the absence of secondary sexual characters).
    • 15 years (regardless of the presence of secondary sexual characters).

     

    Causes of Primary Amenorrhea

    Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
    • Primary ovarian failure
    • Resistant ovarian syndrome
    • Galactosemia

    Developmental defect of genital tract
    • Müllerian agenesis (2nd most common cause)
    • Imperforate hymen (Cryptomenorrhea) 
    • Vaginal agenesis
    • Transverse vaginal septum 

    Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
    • Hypothalamic and pituitary dysfunction
    • Kallmann’s syndrome
    • Craniopharyngioma

    Abnormal chromosomal pattern
    • Turner’s syndrome (most common cause)
    • Pure gonadal dysgenesis
    • Androgen insensitivity syndrome

    Transverse Vaginal Septum - Primary Amenorrhea (Option A): On examination, the hymen would appear normal because the obstruction is higher up in the vaginal canal, not at the introitus.

     

    Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS) - Primary Amenorrhea (Option C): These patients lack a uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina due to normal regression of the Müllerian structures (induced by anti-Müllerian hormone). Therefore, there would be no menstruation and no cyclic abdominal pain. Examination may reveal a short and blind ending vagina.

     

    Müllerian Agenesis - Primary Amenorrhea (Option D): Secondary sexual characteristics develop normally. However, there is an absence of the uterus, upper vagina, and fallopian tubes, so the patient would not experience cyclic abdominal pain as there is no menstruation. The examination would reveal a shortened or absent vagina, not a bluish bulging hymen.

questions.answerText: Halothane is the anesthetic agent of choice in patients with ischaemic heart disease
questions.solution: ong> Halothane is contraindicated in patients with ischaemic heart disease. Halothane decreases cardiac output, BP, and PR Halothane causes hypotension by direct myocardial depression Halothane causes bradycardia by blunting carotid body receptor response Halothane is a common inhalational agent used in the respiratory system (due to maximum bronchodilation) while Isoflurane is the common inhalational agent used in CNS and CVS Central Nervous System: Inhalational agents are CNS depressant They reduce cerebral metabolic rate Commonly used inhalational agent is isoflurane They increase the cerebral blood flow thereby increasing the ICP, so they are avoided in head injury and neurosurgery (maximum with halothane) Isoflurane is an inhalational agent of choice in head injury as it decreases the ICP (Option A) Most epileptogenic agent: Enflurane (increases ICP and also causes epilepsy) Respiratory system Almost all inhalational agents cause bronchodilation (Option C) Reduces the Respiratory rate Causes decreased mucociliary function (except ether) Maximum bronchodilation is seen with halothane, therefore 2nd best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma is halothane. Best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma: Sevoflurane (Option D) Cardiovascular system Reduces heart rate, BP, and systemic vascular resistance Halothane increases the sensitivity of the myocardium toward catecholamines Halothane, isoflurane, enflurane - prolong QT interval Gastrointestinal system: Reduces the liver blood flow Halothane hepatitis: maximally metabolized produces trifluoroacetic acid as an end product that reacts with liver cells (immunologically) causing acute fulminant hepatic necrosis. Uterus: All agents are good uterine relaxants so there is a high chance of PPH @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>

Halothane is contraindicated in patients with ischaemic heart disease.

  • Halothane decreases cardiac output, BP, and PR
  • Halothane causes hypotension by direct myocardial depression
  • Halothane causes bradycardia by blunting carotid body receptor response
  • Halothane is a common inhalational agent used in the respiratory system (due to maximum bronchodilation) while Isoflurane is the common inhalational agent used in CNS and CVS

Central Nervous System:

  • Inhalational agents are CNS depressant
  • They reduce cerebral metabolic rate
  • Commonly used inhalational agent is isoflurane
  • They increase the cerebral blood flow thereby increasing the ICP, so they are avoided in head injury and neurosurgery (maximum with halothane)
  • Isoflurane is an inhalational agent of choice in head injury as it decreases the ICP (Option A)
  • Most epileptogenic agent: Enflurane (increases ICP and also causes epilepsy)

Respiratory system

  • Almost all inhalational agents cause bronchodilation (Option C)
  • Reduces the Respiratory rate
  • Causes decreased mucociliary function (except ether)
  • Maximum bronchodilation is seen with halothane, therefore 2nd best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma is halothane.
  • Best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma: Sevoflurane (Option D)

Cardiovascular system

  • Reduces heart rate, BP, and systemic vascular resistance
  • Halothane increases the sensitivity of the myocardium toward catecholamines
  • Halothane, isoflurane, enflurane - prolong QT interval

Gastrointestinal system:

  • Reduces the liver blood flow
  • Halothane hepatitis: maximally metabolized produces trifluoroacetic acid as an end product that reacts with liver cells (immunologically) causing acute fulminant hepatic necrosis.

Uterus:

  • All agents are good uterine relaxants so there is a high chance of PPH

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the Delphi technique?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements best describes the Delphi technique?

options.label: A
options.text: A method of data collection where participants discuss and agree on a topic in person.

options.label: B
options.text: A qualitative research method that involves direct observation of participants in their natural environment.

options.label: C
options.text: A structured communication technique used in health research that relies on a panel of experts answering questionnaires in multiple rounds to achieve consensus.

options.label: D
options.text: A statistical analysis method used to interpret large datasets through the use of complex algorithms.

questions.answerText: A structured communication technique used in health research that relies on a panel of experts answering questionnaires in multiple rounds to achieve consensus.
questions.solution: Delphi method is a structured communication method that depends on a panel of experts. It involves gathering opinions from the panel of experts on a specific issue, summarizing their collective feedback, and repeating this process for several rounds. After each round, the experts share their feedback and the reasoning behind their judgements anonymously. This feedback encourages experts to reconsider and potentially revise their earlier opinions based on the responses of other panel members. Through this process, the range of responses tends to narrow, and the group will reach a consensus. The Delphi method does not involve participants discussing the issues (Option A) or natural observation (Option B) or statistical analysis (Option D). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
777197e63abf9bf5">Rectouterine pouch → Pelvic abscess

 

Explanation:

Pus moves from the lesser sac through the foramen of Winslow into the greater sac, enters the hepatorenal pouch of Morrison, continues through the paracolic gutter, then reaches the rectouterine pouch of Douglas, where a pelvic abscess may form.

Peritoneal Spaces:

  • Greater Sac:
    • Largest compartment of the peritoneal cavity, spanning the entire abdomen.
  • Lesser Sac:
    • Smaller compartment, located behind the stomach, liver, and lesser omentum, as a diverticulum from the greater sac.
    • Both the sacs can be connected through the foramen of Winslow.
  • Paracolic Gutters:
    • Right Paracolic Gutter:
      • Located lateral to the ascending colon, continuous with the hepatorenal pouch (Morrison’s pouch) above and pelvic cavity below.
      • Infections may spread from the appendix or hepatorenal pouch.
    • Left Paracolic Gutter:
      • Located lateral to the descending colon, limited by the phrenicocolic ligament above, and continuous with the pelvic cavity below.
      • Infections may spread upward from the pelvis.
  • Subphrenic Spaces:
    • Six spaces near the liver, important for surgeons due to frequent pus collection (subphrenic abscesses).
    • Right side:
      • Right posterior intraperitoneal compartment (Hepatorenal pouch or Morrison's pouch).
      • Right anterior intraperitoneal compartment.
      • Right extraperitoneal compartment.
    • Left side:
      • Left posterior intraperitoneal compartment.
      • Left anterior intraperitoneal compartment.
      • Left extraperitoneal compartment.
  • Hepatorenal Pouch (Morison’s Pouch):
    • Located between the liver and right kidney, communicates with the lesser sac through the epiploic foramen.
    • Most dependent part in the supine position, often collecting pus after upper abdominal surgery (e.g., cholecystectomy).
    • Communicates with the rectouterine pouch via the right paracolic gutter, serving as a route for infection from the abdomen to the pelvis.

questions.solution: sentation and absence of bacteria on Gram stain suggest Chlamydia trachomatis as the likely cause of non-gonococcal cervicitis . The first-line treatment is a single dose of Azithromycin (1g orally). The diagnosis of NGU/NGC requires the exclusion of gonorrheal infection. This can be achieved with a gram stain that lacks gram-negative diplococci or by any negative gonorrhea test (culture, nucleic acid testing, among others). Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D-K are the most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis. In females, it can cause various manifestations such as: Mucopurulent cervicitis ( most common ). It may progress to endometritis, salpingitis (fallopian tube), pelvic inflammatory disease, and finally pelvic peritonitis. Perihepatitis ( Fitz–Hugh–Curtis syndrome ). First-line management involves a single oral dose of azithromycin 1g stat. It is preferred due to its greater effectiveness and lower cost . The table below shows the management of uncomplicated chlamydial infections: Non-pregnant First line: Azithromycin 1g single dose Second line: Doxycycline 100mg BD x 7 days Third line: Ofloxacin 200-300mg BD x 7 days Pregnancy First line: Azithromycin 1g oral single dose Second line: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS x 7 days Ceftriaxone (Option B) is used for the treatment of gonococcal infections. Fluconazole (Option C) is used for the treatment of vaginal candidiasis. Doxycycline (Option D) is also highly effective for treating uncomplicated chlamydial infections. questions.solution: p> Drug A has the highest efficacy with the highest potency. Drug B is more potent than drug C. Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce, represented by the Vmax /y-axis value. The higher the Vmax, the higher the efficacy. Potency is the amount of drug required to produce a given effect. The lower the drug dose needed, the higher the potency. Both are independent of each other; efficacious drugs can have high or low potency and vice versa. The first graph helps us estimate the efficacy of the drugs (the higher the Vmax, the higher the efficacy). Thus, Drug A > B >C >D. The second graph helps us estimate the drugs' potency (The lower the drug dose needed, the higher the potency). The left shift of the graph indicates an increase in potency. Thus Drug D > B > C > A. @Neet_pg_bot

  • The first graph helps us estimate the efficacy of the drugs (the higher the Vmax, the higher the efficacy). Thus, Drug A > B >C >D.
  • The second graph helps us estimate the drugs' potency (The lower the drug dose needed, the higher the potency). The left shift of the graph indicates an increase in potency. Thus Drug D > B > C > A.

questions.solution: o and given image suggest ingestion of Ricinus seeds. Ricin , a highly toxic protein derived from the seeds of Ricinus communis , blocks RNA Polymerase and inhibits protein synthesis. Ricinus Communis (Castor): Seeds are smooth, flattened-oval, and mottled with light and dark brown markings. They have a bright, polished finish. Toxicity: The entire plant is toxic due to the water-soluble glycoprotein toxalbumin Ricin , a potent allergen with the highest concentration found in the seeds. The seeds are not toxic if intact but it is toxic if crushed or chewed. Mechanism of action: Ricin inhibits protein synthesis by blocking RNA polymerase . Clinical Features: Symptoms may appear within 10 hours after ingestion. Gastrointestinal: Burning throat pain, abdominal cramps, nausea, thirst, vomiting, and often bloody diarrhea. Central Nervous System: Vertigo, drowsiness, delirium, convulsions, and coma. Other Symptoms include uremia, jaundice, rapid weak pulse, cold, clammy skin, and dehydration. In some cases, consciousness may be retained until death. Fatal Dose: 1–10 µg/kg body weight (inhalation or injection); approximately 2 mg/kg (10–20 seeds) through ingestion. Fatal Period: 3–5 days. Ingestion of castor oil during pregnancy has been associated with teratogenic effects, including growth retardation, craniofacial dysmorphia, limb deformities, vertebral segmentation defects, and seizures in some cases. Treatment: No specific antidotes exist for toxalbumen exposures. Decontamination : Stomach wash, activated charcoal, and catharsis. Supportive Care : IV fluids and monitoring for hypoglycemia and complications of hypovolemia. Urine alkalinisation may help prevent the crystallisation of haemoglobin in severe cases @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: 21β-hydroxylase deficiency leads to reduced cortisol and aldosterone production, causing elevated ACTH and increased production of androgens, resulting in virilization and ambiguous genitalia. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) Definition: Group of genetic disorders affecting adrenal glands, causing enzyme deficiencies in steroid biosynthesis. Effects: Disruption in cortisol and aldosterone production, leading to various symptoms. Prevalence: Most common deficiency is 21β-hydroxylase deficiency (90%+ cases). 21β-Hydroxylase Deficiency Impact: Reduced cortisol and aldosterone production. Consequence: Increased ACTH secretion. (Option B) Result: Increased precursor steroids converted to androgens → Virilization. Steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein deficiency Known as congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia. Prevents cholesterol movement into mitochondria. Low steroid production, female genitalia regardless of genetic sex. 3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency Increases DHEA secretion (weak androgen). Masculinization in females, hypospadias in males. (Option C) 17α-Hydroxylase deficiency Caused by mutated CYP17 gene. Prevents sex hormone production. Female external genitalia, hypertension, hypokalemia due to high 11-deoxycorticosterone. questions.solutionHtml:
21β-hydroxylase deficiency leads to reduced cortisol and aldosterone production, causing elevated ACTH and increased production of androgens, resulting in virilization and ambiguous genitalia.

 

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)

  • Definition: Group of genetic disorders affecting adrenal glands, causing enzyme deficiencies in steroid biosynthesis.
  • Effects: Disruption in cortisol and aldosterone production, leading to various symptoms.
  • Prevalence: Most common deficiency is 21β-hydroxylase deficiency (90%+ cases).

21β-Hydroxylase Deficiency

  • Impact: Reduced cortisol and aldosterone production.
  • Consequence: Increased ACTH secretion. (Option B)
  • Result: Increased precursor steroids converted to androgens → Virilization.

Other Enzyme Deficiencies in CAH

Enzyme Deficiency

Description

Symptoms/Consequences

Cholesterol desmolase deficiency

Fatal in utero, prevents placental progesterone synthesis.

Death before birth.

Steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein deficiency

Known as congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia. Prevents cholesterol movement into mitochondria.

Low steroid production, female genitalia regardless of genetic sex.

3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency

Increases DHEA secretion (weak androgen).

Masculinization in females, hypospadias in males. (Option C)

17α-Hydroxylase deficiency

Caused by mutated CYP17 gene. Prevents sex hormone production.

Female external genitalia, hypertension, hypokalemia due to high 11-deoxycorticosterone. (Option D- not early virilization)

11β-Hydroxylase deficiency

Increased 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone secretion.

Virilization, hypertension due to salt and water retention. (Option A)

Treatment

  • Glucocorticoid treatment: Recommended for all virilizing forms of CAH.
    • Purpose: Addresses glucocorticoid deficit.
    • Effect: Inhibits ACTH secretion, reducing androgen and steroid production.

    CO2 washout due to hyperventilation
    • Treat underlying cause (e.g., fever, sepsis, asthma)

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with a history of asthma is undergoing elective surgery. He is induced with isoflurane and given succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Within minutes, the surgical team observes that he has developed severe muscle rigidity, a rapid heart rate, and a notable increase in body temperature. Which drug/s is/are most likely responsible for the onset of these symptoms in this patient?
questions.solution: lcholine Explanation: In this case, the diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia is typically made based on the presence of characteristic clinical signs—such as muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and hyperthermia—following exposure to certain anaesthetic agents. Both isoflurane (an inhaled anaesthetic) and succinylcholine (a depolarizing muscle relaxant) are well-known triggers for malignant hyperthermia. The combination of these agents heightens the risk of developing this serious condition, which is indicated by the rapid onset of symptoms in the patient after their administration. Triggers of Malignant Hyperthermia: Inhaled general anesthetics Ether Halothane Enflurane Isoflurane Desflurane Sevoflurane Depolarizing muscle relaxant Succinylcholine Prior exercise, even just an hour before anaesthesia induction, intensifies the severity and accelerates the onset of rigidity. Initial Indicators of Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) During Anesthesia: Muscle rigidity Masseter spasm Tachycardia Unexplained hypercarbia Increased temperature Other Features: Cyanosis, metabolic acidosis, hypertension, fever, sweating, Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Myoglobinemia, Myoglobinuria, Cardiac Arrest, DIC, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

lcholine

  • The combination of these agents heightens the risk of developing this serious condition, which is indicated by the rapid onset of symptoms in the patient after their administration.

 

Triggers of Malignant Hyperthermia:

  • Inhaled general anesthetics
    • Ether
    • Halothane
    • Enflurane
    • Isoflurane
    • Desflurane
    • Sevoflurane
  • Depolarizing muscle relaxant

  • Prior exercise, even just an hour before anaesthesia induction, intensifies the severity and accelerates the onset of rigidity.

 

Initial Indicators of Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) During Anesthesia:

  • Masseter spasm
  • Tachycardia
  • Unexplained hypercarbia
  • Increased temperature

 

Other Features:

  • Cyanosis, metabolic acidosis, hypertension, fever, sweating,
  • Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Myoglobinemia, Myoglobinuria, Cardiac Arrest, DIC, etc.

questions.stemHtml:
A 55 year-old male presents to the emergency department with fever, tachypnea, and altered mental status. BP is 100/60 mm Hg
Laboratory results show:
	WBC: 14,000/μL
	Serum lactate: 1.8 mmol/L
	Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
Chest X-ray reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate. The patient requires 6 L/min of oxygen to maintain  pO2 of 90 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: Answer is B: Sepsis According to the Sepsis-3 criteria , sepsis is defined as a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The clinical criteria for sepsis include: Suspected infection An acute increase of ≥ 2 point in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) In this case: The patient has a suspected lung infection (fever and chest X-ray infiltrate). There is evidence of organ dysfunction: Respiratory: PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 200 . PaO₂ = 90 mm Hg Oxygen flow rate = 6 L/min via nasal cannula Estimated FiO₂ at 6 L/min ≈ 45% = 0.45 so PaO2/FiO2= 90/0.45 = 200 Renal: Creatinine increase > 0.3 mg/dL from baseline This meets the Sepsis-3 criteria for sepsis. SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) Score: The SOFA score is a more comprehensive tool used to assess organ dysfunction in potentially septic patients. It evaluates six organ systems: Respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 ratio) Cardiovascular (Mean arterial pressure and vasopressor requirements) Hepatic (Bilirubin level) Coagulation (Platelet count) Renal (Creatinine level or urine output) Neurological (Glasgow Coma Scale) Each system is scored from 0 to 4, with higher scores indicating more severe dysfunction. A total SOFA score ranges from 0 to 24. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Answer is B: Sepsis 

According to the Sepsis-3 criteria , sepsis is defined as a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The clinical criteria for sepsis include:

  1. Suspected infection
  2. An acute increase of ≥2  point in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment)  

In this case:

  • The patient has a suspected lung infection (fever and chest X-ray infiltrate).
  • There is evidence of organ dysfunction:
    • Respiratory: PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 200 . PaO₂ = 90 mm Hg

    • Oxygen flow rate = 6 L/min via nasal cannula

    • Estimated FiO₂ at 6 L/min ≈ 45% = 0.45

    • so PaO2/FiO2= 90/0.45 = 200 

    • Renal: Creatinine increase > 0.3 mg/dL from baseline

This meets the Sepsis-3 criteria for sepsis.

 

SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) Score:

The SOFA score is a more comprehensive tool used to assess organ dysfunction in potentially septic patients. It evaluates six organ systems:

  1. Respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 ratio)
  2. Cardiovascular (Mean arterial pressure and vasopressor requirements)
  3. Hepatic (Bilirubin level)
  4. Coagulation (Platelet count)
  5. Renal (Creatinine level or urine output)
  6. Neurological (Glasgow Coma Scale)

Each system is scored from 0 to 4, with higher scores indicating more severe dysfunction. A total SOFA score ranges from 0 to 24.

questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following steps in the Citric acid cycle involves oxidative phosphorylation and decarboxylation?
	Isocitrate → α-Ketoglutarate
	Succinate → Fumarate
	Malate → Oxaloacetate
	α-Ketoglutarate → Succinyl-CoA
questions.solution: The enzymes involved in both reactions are Isocitrate Dehydrogenase (Step 1) and α-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase (Step 4). Both involve oxidation and removal of CO₂ and produce NADH, which is later used in oxidative phosphorylation. Steps 3 and 4 are catalysed by Succinate dehydrogenase, and Malate Dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of malate to oxaloacetate, producing NADH, which enters oxidative phosphorylation. Oxidation reactions contribute to the Electron Transport Chain by generating NADH/FADH₂ . Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs at the Succinyl-CoA to Succinate step. Hydration reaction occurs when Fumarase converts Fumarate to Malate . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A forensic investigator is analyzing a crime scene for potential blood stains. questions.stemHtml: A forensic investigator is analyzing a crime scene for potential blood stains. They decide to use a presumptive test that can detect trace amounts of blood but may also give false positives with other substances like bleach or rust. Which of the following is the most appropriate test for this scenario?
questions.solution: g> is widely used for detecting trace amounts of blood. It reacts with hemoglobin and produces a chemiluminescent glow in the dark. However, it can yield false positives with substances like bleach or metals. Blood Stain Screening Tests in Forensic Medicine Presumptive Tests Luminol : Detects trace blood stains by reacting with hemoglobin. Produces a chemiluminescent glow in the dark. Prone to false positives (e.g., with metals or bleach). Forensic Bluestar : (Option D ruled out) Offers rapid results and can be used for DNA analysis afterward. Similar to Luminol but also has a risk of false positives. Kastle Meyer Test : (Option A ruled out) High specificity but lower sensitivity. Detects blood at 1:16,384 dilution. Hemastix : (Option B ruled out) More sensitive than Kastle Meyer (detects blood at 1:64 dilution). Less specific, with false positives from substances like tomatoes or rust. Principles of Blood Detection Tests: Test Working Principle Kastle-Meyer Hemoglobin catalyzes the oxidation of phenolphthalein, resulting in a pink color. Hemastix Reagent reacts with hemoglobin, causing a color change based on the concentration of hemoglobin. Luminol Chemiluminescent reaction occurs when luminol reacts with hemoglobin under alkaline conditions, producing a blue glow. Forensic Bluestar Similar to luminol, but with enhanced sensitivity; it reacts with hemoglobin to produce a bright blue luminescence. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
g> is widely used for detecting trace amounts of blood.
  • It reacts with hemoglobin and produces a chemiluminescent glow in the dark.
  • However, it can yield false positives with substances like bleach or metals.

    •  

    Blood Stain Screening Tests in Forensic Medicine

    Presumptive Tests

    • Luminol:
      • Detects trace blood stains by reacting with hemoglobin.
      • Produces a chemiluminescent glow in the dark.
      • Prone to false positives (e.g., with metals or bleach).

    • Forensic Bluestar: (Option D ruled out)
      • Offers rapid results and can be used for DNA analysis afterward.
      • Similar to Luminol but also has a risk of false positives.
    • Kastle Meyer Test: (Option A ruled out)
      • High specificity but lower sensitivity.
      • Detects blood at 1:16,384 dilution.
    • Hemastix: (Option B ruled out)
      • More sensitive than Kastle Meyer (detects blood at 1:64 dilution).
      • Less specific, with false positives from substances like tomatoes or rust.

    Principles of Blood Detection Tests:

    Test

    Working Principle

    Kastle-Meyer

    Hemoglobin catalyzes the oxidation of phenolphthalein, resulting in a pink color.

    Hemastix

    Reagent reacts with hemoglobin, causing a color change based on the concentration of hemoglobin.

    Luminol

    Chemiluminescent reaction occurs when luminol reacts with hemoglobin under alkaline conditions, producing a blue glow.

    Forensic Bluestar

    Similar to luminol, but with enhanced sensitivity; it reacts with hemoglobin to produce a bright blue luminescence.

questions.stem: A 3 year old child presents with swelling and pain in the region of the parotid gland, accompanied by ear discharge. Examination of the external auditory canal (EAC) reveals signs of infection. Which bony anatomical structure is responsible for the spread of infection between the EAC and the parotid gland?
questions.stemHtml: A 3 year old child presents with swelling and pain in the region of the parotid gland, accompanied by ear discharge. Examination of the external auditory canal (EAC) reveals signs of infection. Which bony anatomical structure is responsible for the spread of infection between the EAC and the parotid gland?
questions.solution: e: A deficiency in the anteroinferior bony EAC, present in some children under four and occasionally into adulthood. It allows infection to spread between the parotid gland and the EAC. (Option B) Fissures of Santorini: Two gaps in the cartilage of the outer EAC that allow infection to pass between the parotid glands and the EAC. Isthmus: A narrowing in the bony EAC, about 6 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane. It is not an opening but a constriction in the canal. (Option C) Tympanic membrane (Option D) : The tympanic membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear and is not involved in spreading infections to the parotid gland. Mastoid Air Cells (Option A) : Mastoid air cells are a series of air-filled spaces located within the mastoid process of the temporal bone, adjacent to the middle ear. While infections in the middle ear (otitis media) can spread to the mastoid air cells (causing mastoiditis), they do not directly connect the EAC to the parotid gland. Thus, they are not responsible for the spread of infection between these two areas. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
e: A deficiency in the anteroinferior bony EAC, present in some children under four and occasionally into adulthood.
  • It allows infection to spread between the parotid gland and the EAC. (Option B)
  • Fissures of Santorini: Two gaps in the cartilage of the outer EAC that allow infection to pass between the parotid glands and the EAC.
  • Isthmus: A narrowing in the bony EAC, about 6 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane. It is not an opening but a constriction in the canal. (Option C)

    • Tympanic membrane (Option D):

    • The tympanic membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear and is not involved in spreading infections to the parotid gland.

    Mastoid Air Cells (Option A):

    • Mastoid air cells are a series of air-filled spaces located within the mastoid process of the temporal bone, adjacent to the middle ear.
    • While infections in the middle ear (otitis media) can spread to the mastoid air cells (causing mastoiditis), they do not directly connect the EAC to the parotid gland.
    • Thus, they are not responsible for the spread of infection between these two areas.

questions.solutionHtml:
ate agar supplemented with vancomycin is the optimal culture medium, providing necessary nutrients and inhibiting normal flora.

H. ducreyi:

  • Gram-negative coccobacillus
  • It causes painful genital ulcers with ragged edges and a purulent base.
  • Fastidious, requiring X factor only and not V factor
  • Organisms are arranged one behind the other, giving characteristic "school of fish" or "railroad track" arrangements in Gram stains
  • Individually, each bacterium shows bipolar staining, known as the safety pin appearance.
  • For culture, chocolate agar is used but requires special supplements such as IsoVitalex, fetal calf serum, or vancomycin-enriched chocolate agar.

 

 

"Pushing test" is diagnostic; further laboratory confirmation unnecessary (Option B): The "pushing test" is suggestive but not diagnostic for chancroid. Laboratory confirmation is still necessary.

 

Multiplex PCR is less sensitive than culture for diagnosis (Option C): Multiplex PCR is more sensitive than culture for H. ducreyi diagnosis, not less.

 

Single-dose azithromycin; partner treatment optional if asymptomatic (Option D): While single-dose azithromycin is a recommended treatment, partner treatment is necessary regardless of symptoms.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following breast lesions are correctly paired with their histopathological characteristics? 1. Fibrocystic changes 2. Duct ectasia 3. Phyllodes tumor 4. Invasive Ductal Carcinoma
questions.solution: "> Fibrocystic changes Cysts: Fluid-filled sacs within the breast tissue, often surrounded by fibrous tissue. Fibrosis: Thickening and scarring of breast tissue, which may result in palpable lumps or areas of increased density on imaging studies. Apocrine Metaplasia: Transformation of ductal epithelial cells into apocrine-like cells, characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical snouts. Duct ectasia A lot of foamy macrophages, periductal lymphocytic infiltrates can be observed. Phyllodes tumor Increased stromal cellularity and overgrowth, giving rise to the typical leaf-like architecture. Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) Types of DCIS: Micropapillary tumors : Additional epithelial cells within the lumen. Cribriform tumors: Ducts filled with cells that form multiple lumena. Solid tumors: Completely filled ducts. Comedo tumors: Solid with a necrotic core Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC) Shows more mucin both extracellular and intracellular with signet ring cells. Fibroadenoma Well-defined borders due to a fibrous capsule , with proliferating stroma potentially compressing and distorting glandular components. Intracanalicular fibroadenoma - Ducts are compressed. Pericanalicular fibroadenoma - Ducts are open. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
">

Fibrocystic changes

Cysts: Fluid-filled sacs within the breast tissue, often surrounded by fibrous tissue.

Fibrosis: Thickening and scarring of breast tissue, which may result in palpable lumps or areas of increased density on imaging studies.

Apocrine Metaplasia: Transformation of ductal epithelial cells into apocrine-like cells, characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical snouts.

Duct ectasia

A lot of foamy macrophages, periductal lymphocytic infiltrates can be observed.

Phyllodes tumor

Increased stromal cellularity and overgrowth, giving rise to the typical leaf-like architecture.

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS)

Types of DCIS:

  • Micropapillary tumors: Additional epithelial cells within the lumen.
  • Cribriform tumors: Ducts filled with cells that form multiple lumena.
  • Solid tumors: Completely filled ducts.
  • Comedo tumors: Solid with a necrotic core

Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC)

Shows more mucin both extracellular and intracellular with signet ring cells.

Fibroadenoma

Well-defined borders due to a fibrous capsule, with proliferating stroma potentially compressing and distorting glandular components.

  • Intracanalicular fibroadenoma - Ducts are compressed.

  • Pericanalicular fibroadenoma - Ducts are open.

Physical examination reveals tense ascites, mild jaundice, and peripheral edema. Laboratory investigations show: Serum creatinine: 2.3 mg/dL (baseline: 0.9 mg/dL) Serum sodium: 126 mEq/L Urine sodium: <10 mEq/L Albumin infusion is planned as part of his management. What is the recommended dosage of albumin infusion for this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 56-year-old man with a history of cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C presents with worsening ascites, oliguria, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals tense ascites, mild jaundice, and peripheral edema. Laboratory investigations show:
Serum creatinine: 2.3 mg/dL (baseline: 0.9 mg/dL)
Serum sodium: 126 mEq/L
Urine sodium: &lt;10 mEq/L
Albumin infusion is planned as part of his management. What is the recommended dosage of albumin infusion for this patient?
questions.solution: s Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS), a complication of advanced liver disease characterized by renal dysfunction due to splanchnic vasodilation and reduced renal perfusion. HRS is diagnosed based on clinical features, including worsening renal function, low urine sodium (<10 mEq/L), and exclusion of other causes of acute kidney injury (e.g., hypovolemia, nephrotoxicity). The recommended dosage of albumin infusion in HRS is 1 g/kg per day, up to a maximum of 100 g/day, to expand intravascular volume and improve renal perfusion. This is used in combination with vasoconstrictors like terlipressin or norepinephrine to reverse the underlying renal vasoconstriction. Higher doses (e.g., 2-5 g/kg/day) are avoided due to risks such as pulmonary edema. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man has been complaining of fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and swelling in his ankles and legs over the past few months. On physical examination, you notice hepatomegaly and proteinuria. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum creatinine levels and microscopic hematuria. Which of the following types of amyloid is most likely responsible for this patient's presentation?
questions.solution: also known as primary systemic amyloidosis , is characterized by the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (lambda or kappa) produced by clonal plasma cells. In this type of amyloidosis, the deposited amyloid fibrils can infiltrate various organs and tissues, including the kidneys, leading to organ dysfunction. Clinical manifestations commonly include Renal involvement causing proteinuria and renal impairment Hepatomegaly Peripheral oedema due to cardiac involvement. AA amyloidosis (Option A): AA amyloidosis, also known as secondary systemic amyloidosis, occurs secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, or chronic infections. In AA amyloidosis, the amyloid fibrils are derived from serum amyloid A protein, an acute-phase reactant synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes in response to inflammation. AB amyloidosis (Option B): AB amyloidosis is not a recognized subtype of amyloidosis. Amyloid fibrils derived from A Beta peptide are associated with Alzheimer's disease, but they are not a primary cause of systemic amyloidosis involving multiple organs. ATTR amyloidosis (Option D): ATTR amyloidosis, also known as transthyretin amyloidosis, occurs due to the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from transthyretin protein, a transporter of thyroxine and retinol-binding protein. It can be hereditary (caused by mutations in the transthyretin gene) or acquired (due to wild-type transthyretin protein). It typically affects the heart and peripheral nerves, leading to cardiomyopathy and peripheral neuropathy, respectively. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for inhibiting motor neuron activity at the level of the spinal cord to regulate muscle tone and reflexes?
questions.stemHtml: Which neurotransmitter is primarily responsible for inhibiting motor neuron activity at the level of the spinal cord to regulate muscle tone and reflexes?
questions.solution: pan class="customMeta" data-dictid="d816ba952f1692777199fc69bd7c56">spinal cord level: Glycine acts as a primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. It plays a crucial role in regulating motor neuron activity by hyperpolarising postsynaptic neurons, thereby reducing their excitability. Dysfunction or deficiency in glycine can lead to increased motor neuron excitability, resulting in symptoms such as muscle spasms and exaggerated reflexes. In CNS: Glycine has both inhibitory and excitatory action in the central nervous system. A small amount of extracellular glycine is essential for the proper functioning of the NMDA channel. Although glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, it is necessary to activate the NMDA receptor, which plays a role in excitatory neurotransmission. GABA (Option A) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter primarily found in the brain and less involved in spinal motor neuron regulation than glycine. Glutamate (Option B) is an excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain that facilitates neuronal signalling. Acetylcholine (Option D) is involved in neuromuscular transmission at the neuromuscular junction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 52 year old chronic alcoholic presents to the ED with confusion, difficulty walking, and abnormal eye movements. He reports having consumed large amounts of alcohol daily for many years and has had poor dietary intake. On examination, he has nystagmus and an unsteady gait. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: The patient's symptoms of confusion, difficulty walking (cerebellar ataxia), and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) are classic signs of Wernicke encephalopathy , which is caused by thiamine deficiency often seen in chronic alcoholics. Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (Cerebral Beriberi) Clinical Manifestations Wernicke Encephalopathy: Symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, global confusion. Korsakoff Psychosis: Symptoms: Anterograde and retrograde amnesia, sensory agnosia, and confabulation. (Option B ruled out) Causes of Thiamine Deficiency in Alcoholics Increased thiamine requirements due to alcohol consumption. Impaired intestinal absorption of thiamine due to alcohol. Increased thiamine utilization and inadequate dietary intake. Inhibition of intestinal thiamine absorption by alcohol. Metabolic Implications Impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Accumulation of pyruvate and lactate in the blood. Potential for life-threatening lactic acidosis. Progression and Risk Factors Progression from Wernicke encephalopathy to Korsakoff psychosis if untreated. Associated with severely compromised nutritional status, often due to chronic alcoholism. MRI findings Symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the mammillary bodies, dorsomedial thalami, periaqueductal gray matter, and around the third ventricle. Lactic acidosis (Option C): While thiamine deficiency can lead to an accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, resulting in lactic acidosis, the clinical presentation of confusion, ataxia, and nystagmus is more indicative of Wernicke encephalopathy. Lactic acidosis might be present but is not the primary diagnosis based on the symptoms described. Dry beriberi (Option D) primarily affects the peripheral nervous system, causing peripheral neuritis, paresthesia, foot drop, muscle weakness, and distal sensory loss. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The patient's symptoms of confusion, difficulty walking (cerebellar ataxia), and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) are classic signs of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is caused by thiamine deficiency often seen in chronic alcoholics.

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (Cerebral Beriberi)

Clinical Manifestations

Wernicke Encephalopathy:

Symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, global confusion.

Korsakoff Psychosis:

Symptoms: Anterograde and retrograde amnesia, sensory agnosia, and confabulation. (Option B ruled out)

Causes of Thiamine Deficiency in Alcoholics
  • Increased thiamine requirements due to alcohol consumption. Impaired intestinal absorption of thiamine due to alcohol. Increased thiamine utilization and inadequate dietary intake.
  • Inhibition of intestinal thiamine absorption by alcohol.

Metabolic Implications
  • Impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
  • Accumulation of pyruvate and lactate in the blood.
  • Potential for life-threatening lactic acidosis.

Progression and Risk Factors
  • Progression from Wernicke encephalopathy to Korsakoff psychosis if untreated.
  • Associated with severely compromised nutritional status, often due to chronic alcoholism.

MRI findings

 Symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the mammillary bodies, dorsomedial thalami, periaqueductal gray matter, and around the third ventricle.

Lactic acidosis (Option C): While thiamine deficiency can lead to an accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, resulting in lactic acidosis, the clinical presentation of confusion, ataxia, and nystagmus is more indicative of Wernicke encephalopathy. Lactic acidosis might be present but is not the primary diagnosis based on the symptoms described.

Dry beriberi (Option D) primarily affects the peripheral nervous system, causing peripheral neuritis, paresthesia, foot drop, muscle weakness, and distal sensory loss.

Definition

  • Benign tumours arising from the proliferation of glandular tissue in the breast

Prevalence

  • Most common in women aged 15-25 years

Aetiology

  • Believed to be influenced by hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years

Clinical Presentation

  • Painless, firm, rubbery, and mobile lumps
  • Described as feeling like a "marble in the breast"

Diagnosis

  • Triple Assessment: Clinical examination, radiological imaging (ultrasound), tissue sampling (core-needle biopsy)
  • Ultrasound: Helps distinguish fibroadenomas from cysts
  • Core-Needle Biopsy: Provides definitive diagnosis

Treatment

  • Conservative Management: Watchful waiting, regular monitoring(Option B)
  • Giant Fibroadenomas: Over 5 cm, may require excision through submammary incision (Option C)
